Conditioning on Random Variables and the Law of Iterated Expectation

This topic covers Lectures 11–13. You condition a random variable on an event, on a partition, or on another random variable, and get a new PMF or PDF. Averaging those conditional answers back gives the total probability theorem for distributions and the law of iterated expectation E[X]=E[E[X∣Y]]E[X]=E\big[E[X\mid Y]\big]E[X]=E[E[X∣Y]]. The mid-sem asks this every year, usually as 6–10 marks: a conditional density from a joint density, a random sum, a Poisson with a random parameter, or a Gaussian mixture. In the end-sem it is about one question per paper: the mixture X=YZX=Y_ZX=YZ​ (2025, 10 marks) and a random geometric sum (2022). Expect a short, rubric-driven question: name the theorem you condition with, find the conditional law, then average. A printable question list (PDF) has every question below with a tick box.

What is inside

    1  Conditioning on an event · Lecture 11

    Theory recap

    Once an event AAA with P(A)>0P(A)\gt 0P(A)>0 has happened, every probability is re-measured inside AAA. For a random variable this gives a new PMF or PDF that lives only on the part of the range compatible with AAA.

    Conditional PMF / PDF given an event

    pX∣A(x)=P({X=x}∩A)P(A),∑xpX∣A(x)=1.p_{X\mid A}(x)=\frac{P(\{X=x\}\cap A)}{P(A)},\qquad \sum_x p_{X\mid A}(x)=1.pX∣A​(x)=P(A)P({X=x}∩A)​,x∑​pX∣A​(x)=1. If the event is about XXX itself, A={X∈B}A=\{X\in B\}A={X∈B}, then pX∣A(x)={pX(x)P(X∈B),x∈B,0,x∉B,fX∣A(x)={fX(x)P(X∈B),x∈B,0,x∉B.p_{X\mid A}(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{p_X(x)}{P(X\in B)}, & x\in B,\\[4pt] 0, & x\notin B,\end{cases}\qquad f_{X\mid A}(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{f_X(x)}{P(X\in B)}, & x\in B,\\[4pt] 0, & x\notin B.\end{cases}pX∣A​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​P(X∈B)pX​(x)​,0,​x∈B,x∈/B,​fX∣A​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​P(X∈B)fX​(x)​,0,​x∈B,x∈/B.​ Same shape as before, cut to BBB, and rescaled so it integrates to 1. The conditional CDF is FX∣A(x)=P(X≤x∣A)F_{X\mid A}(x)=P(X\le x\mid A)FX∣A​(x)=P(X≤x∣A).

    Conditional expectation given an event

    E[X∣A]=∑xx pX∣A(x)or∫−∞∞x fX∣A(x) dx,E[g(X)∣A]=∫g(x)fX∣A(x) dx,E[X\mid A]=\sum_x x\,p_{X\mid A}(x)\quad\text{or}\quad\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x\,f_{X\mid A}(x)\,dx,\qquad E[g(X)\mid A]=\int g(x)f_{X\mid A}(x)\,dx,E[X∣A]=x∑​xpX∣A​(x)or∫−∞∞​xfX∣A​(x)dx,E[g(X)∣A]=∫g(x)fX∣A​(x)dx, and Var(X∣A)=E[X2∣A]−(E[X∣A])2\mathrm{Var}(X\mid A)=E[X^2\mid A]-(E[X\mid A])^2Var(X∣A)=E[X2∣A]−(E[X∣A])2.

    Partitions: total probability and total expectation

    If A1,…,AnA_1,\dots,A_nA1​,…,An​ partition Ω\OmegaΩ and each P(Ai)>0P(A_i)\gt0P(Ai​)>0: pX(x)=∑i=1nP(Ai) pX∣Ai(x),fX(x)=∑i=1nP(Ai) fX∣Ai(x),E[X]=∑i=1nP(Ai) E[X∣Ai].p_X(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i)\,p_{X\mid A_i}(x),\qquad f_X(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i)\,f_{X\mid A_i}(x),\qquad E[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i)\,E[X\mid A_i].pX​(x)=i=1∑n​P(Ai​)pX∣Ai​​(x),fX​(x)=i=1∑n​P(Ai​)fX∣Ai​​(x),E[X]=i=1∑n​P(Ai​)E[X∣Ai​]. The proof of the first is the law of total probability applied to the event {X=x}\{X=x\}{X=x}.

    Lecture example: memorylessness

    N∼N\simN∼ Geometric(p)(p)(p), A={N>n}A=\{N\gt n\}A={N>n}, P(A)=(1−p)nP(A)=(1-p)^nP(A)=(1−p)n. For k>nk\gt nk>n: pN∣A(k)=(1−p)k−1p(1−p)n=(1−p)k−1−npp_{N\mid A}(k)=\dfrac{(1-p)^{k-1}p}{(1-p)^n}=(1-p)^{k-1-n}ppN∣A​(k)=(1−p)n(1−p)k−1p​=(1−p)k−1−np, and 000 for k≤nk\le nk≤n. So N−nN-nN−n given N>nN\gt nN>n is again Geometric(p)(p)(p). The exponential behaves the same way (see RQ22.A4).

    Watch out

    Always state the new support: a conditional PDF written without "for x>1x\gt 1x>1, 0 otherwise" loses the support mark. Divide by P(A)P(A)P(A), not by fXf_XfX​ at a point.

    RQ22.A4Exponential(1) conditioned on X > 1 2022 Replacement Quiz · S1 Q4 · 6 marks★ Must-do
    Let XXX be an exponential random variable with parameter 1. Find
    1. Conditional PDF and CDF given X>1X \gt 1X>1
    2. E[X∣X>1]E[X\mid X\gt 1]E[X∣X>1]
    Solution · follows the official key

    X∼X\simX∼ Exp(1): fX(x)=e−xf_X(x)=e^{-x}fX​(x)=e−x for x>0x\gt 0x>0, and 000 otherwise. Let A={X>1}A=\{X\gt 1\}A={X>1}.

    1. Conditional PDF and CDF

    P(A)=∫1∞e−x dx=e−1=1e.P(A)=\int_1^\infty e^{-x}\,dx=e^{-1}=\frac1e.P(A)=∫1∞​e−xdx=e−1=e1​.     2. Conditional mean

    E[X∣X>1]=∫1∞x e−(x−1) dx=e∫1∞xe−x dx=e[−xe−x−e−x]1∞=e⋅2e=2.E[X\mid X\gt 1]=\int_1^\infty x\,e^{-(x-1)}\,dx=e\int_1^\infty x e^{-x}\,dx=e\Big[-xe^{-x}-e^{-x}\Big]_1^\infty=e\cdot\frac{2}{e}=2.E[X∣X>1]=∫1∞​xe−(x−1)dx=e∫1∞​xe−xdx=e[−xe−x−e−x]1∞​=e⋅e2​=2. (Check: given X>1X\gt1X>1, X−1X-1X−1 is again Exp(1) by memorylessness, so E[X∣X>1]=1+1=2E[X\mid X\gt1]=1+1=2E[X∣X>1]=1+1=2.)

    Answer

    2  Conditional PMFs, PDFs and E[X | Y = y] · Lectures 11–12

    Theory recap

    Conditioning XXX on {Y=y}\{Y=y\}{Y=y} is conditioning on an event, one event for each value yyy. For continuous YYY the event has probability 0, so the conditional density is defined as the ratio below; geometrically it is the slice of the joint density at height yyy, rescaled to area 1.

    Conditional PMF / PDF given Y = y

    pX∣Y(x∣y)=pX,Y(x,y)pY(y),fX∣Y(x∣y)=fX,Y(x,y)fY(y),for y with pY(y)>0 or fY(y)>0.p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)},\qquad f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},\qquad\text{for } y \text{ with } p_Y(y)\gt0 \text{ or } f_Y(y)\gt0.pX∣Y​(x∣y)=pY​(y)pX,Y​(x,y)​,fX∣Y​(x∣y)=fY​(y)fX,Y​(x,y)​,for y with pY​(y)>0 or fY​(y)>0. Equivalently (multiplication rule) fX,Y(x,y)=fX∣Y(x∣y)fY(y)=fY∣X(y∣x)fX(x)f_{X,Y}(x,y)=f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)f_Y(y)=f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)f_X(x)fX,Y​(x,y)=fX∣Y​(x∣y)fY​(y)=fY∣X​(y∣x)fX​(x), and integrating out: fX(x)=∫−∞∞fX∣Y(x∣y)fY(y) dy,pX(x)=∑ypX∣Y(x∣y)pY(y).f_X(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)f_Y(y)\,dy,\qquad p_X(x)=\sum_y p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)p_Y(y).fX​(x)=∫−∞∞​fX∣Y​(x∣y)fY​(y)dy,pX​(x)=y∑​pX∣Y​(x∣y)pY​(y). For fixed yyy, x↦fX∣Y(x∣y)x\mapsto f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)x↦fX∣Y​(x∣y) is a genuine PDF: ∫fX∣Y(x∣y) dx=fY(y)/fY(y)=1\int f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx=f_Y(y)/f_Y(y)=1∫fX∣Y​(x∣y)dx=fY​(y)/fY​(y)=1.

    Conditional expectation and variance given Y = y

    E[X∣Y=y]=∫x fX∣Y(x∣y) dx,E[g(X)∣Y=y]=∫g(x)fX∣Y(x∣y) dx,E[X\mid Y=y]=\int x\,f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx,\qquad E[g(X)\mid Y=y]=\int g(x)f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx,E[X∣Y=y]=∫xfX∣Y​(x∣y)dx,E[g(X)∣Y=y]=∫g(x)fX∣Y​(x∣y)dx, Var(X∣Y=y)=E[X2∣Y=y]−(E[X∣Y=y])2.\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y=y)=E[X^2\mid Y=y]-\big(E[X\mid Y=y]\big)^2.Var(X∣Y=y)=E[X2∣Y=y]−(E[X∣Y=y])2. Each is a number for each fixed yyy; as yyy varies it is a function of yyy.

    Recipe for "joint PDF → conditional" questions
    1. Draw the support. For each fixed yyy, write the xxx-interval (the slice).
    2. Normalising constant: ∬f=1\iint f=1∬f=1.
    3. Marginal fY(y)=∫slicefX,Y(x,y) dxf_Y(y)=\int_{\text{slice}} f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dxfY​(y)=∫slice​fX,Y​(x,y)dx, with its range of yyy.
    4. fX∣Y=fX,Y/fYf_{X\mid Y}=f_{X,Y}/f_YfX∣Y​=fX,Y​/fY​ on the slice, 0 elsewhere, valid for yyy with fY(y)>0f_Y(y)\gt0fY​(y)>0.
    5. Conditional mean/probability: integrate against fX∣Y(⋅∣y)f_{X\mid Y}(\cdot\mid y)fX∣Y​(⋅∣y) over the slice.
    Independence

    X,YX,YX,Y independent   ⟺  fX,Y=fXfY\iff f_{X,Y}=f_Xf_Y⟺fX,Y​=fX​fY​   ⟺  fX∣Y(x∣y)=fX(x)\iff f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=f_X(x)⟺fX∣Y​(x∣y)=fX​(x) for every yyy with fY(y)>0f_Y(y)\gt0fY​(y)>0. A support that is not a product set (a triangle, a diamond) already rules independence out, and so does any conditional that depends on yyy.

    Watch out

    The conditional density must carry its support and the range of yyy where it is defined: "fX∣Y(x∣y)=1/yf_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1/yfX∣Y​(x∣y)=1/y" alone is incomplete; write "1/y1/y1/y for 0<x<y0\lt x\lt y0<x<y, 0 otherwise, for 0<y<10\lt y\lt 10<y<1". A uniform joint density on a region gives uniform conditionals on the slices.

    1. Find the constant ccc that makes fX,Y(x,y)f_{X,Y}(x,y)fX,Y​(x,y) a valid joint pdf. (2 mks)
    2. Find the marginal density functions fX(x)f_X(x)fX​(x) and fY(y)f_Y(y)fY​(y). (2 mks)
    3. Find the conditional density functions fX∣Y(x∣y)f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)fX∣Y​(x∣y) and fY∣X(y∣x)f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)fY∣X​(y∣x). (2 mks)
    4. Compute the conditional expectation E[X∣Y=y]\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]E[X∣Y=y]. (2 mks)
    5. Are XXX and YYY independent? Justify your answer. (2 mks)

    Parts (c) and (d) belong to this topic; (a), (b), (e) are in Topic 4 and are solved briefly here because (c) needs them. Same as: midsem sample bank SB.B2(c)–(d).

    Solution · follows the official key

    (a), (b) (needed for (c))

    ∫01 ⁣∫01(x+y) dx dy=12+12=1\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 (x+y)\,dx\,dy=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1∫01​∫01​(x+y)dxdy=21​+21​=1, so c=1c=1c=1. Then for 0≤x≤10\le x\le10≤x≤1: fX(x)=∫01(x+y) dy=x+12f_X(x)=\int_0^1(x+y)\,dy=x+\tfrac12fX​(x)=∫01​(x+y)dy=x+21​; by symmetry fY(y)=y+12f_Y(y)=y+\tfrac12fY​(y)=y+21​ for 0≤y≤10\le y\le 10≤y≤1 (both 0 outside [0,1][0,1][0,1]).

    (c) Conditional densities

    For 0≤y≤10\le y\le 10≤y≤1 we have fY(y)=y+12>0f_Y(y)=y+\frac12\gt0fY​(y)=y+21​>0, so fX∣Y(x∣y)=fX,Y(x,y)fY(y)={x+yy+12,0≤x≤1,0,otherwise,fY∣X(y∣x)={x+yx+12,0≤y≤1,0,otherwise,f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x+y}{y+\frac12}, & 0\le x\le 1,\\[4pt] 0, &\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\qquad f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x+y}{x+\frac12}, & 0\le y\le 1,\\[4pt] 0, &\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}fX∣Y​(x∣y)=fY​(y)fX,Y​(x,y)​=⎩⎨⎧​y+21​x+y​,0,​0≤x≤1,otherwise,​fY∣X​(y∣x)=⎩⎨⎧​x+21​x+y​,0,​0≤y≤1,otherwise,​ the second for 0≤x≤10\le x\le10≤x≤1.

    (d) Conditional expectation

    E[X∣Y=y]=∫01x x+yy+12 dx=1y+12[x33+yx22]01=13+y2y+12=2+3y3(2y+1),0≤y≤1.E[X\mid Y=y]=\int_0^1 x\,\frac{x+y}{y+\frac12}\,dx=\frac{1}{y+\frac12}\left[\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{yx^2}{2}\right]_0^1=\frac{\frac13+\frac y2}{y+\frac12}=\frac{2+3y}{3(2y+1)},\qquad 0\le y\le1.E[X∣Y=y]=∫01​xy+21​x+y​dx=y+21​1​[3x3​+2yx2​]01​=y+21​31​+2y​​=3(2y+1)2+3y​,0≤y≤1. Sanity check: at y=0y=0y=0 this is 2/32/32/3 (density 2x2x2x), at y=1y=1y=1 it is 5/95/95/9.

    (e)

    fX(x)fY(y)=(x+12)(y+12)≠x+yf_X(x)f_Y(y)=(x+\frac12)(y+\frac12)\ne x+yfX​(x)fY​(y)=(x+21​)(y+21​)=x+y (e.g. at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0): 14≠0\frac14\ne041​=0), so not independent; equivalently fX∣Yf_{X\mid Y}fX∣Y​ depends on yyy.

    Answer

    fX∣Y(x∣y)=x+yy+1/2f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\dfrac{x+y}{y+1/2}fX∣Y​(x∣y)=y+1/2x+y​, fY∣X(y∣x)=x+yx+1/2f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\dfrac{x+y}{x+1/2}fY∣X​(y∣x)=x+1/2x+y​ on the unit square; E[X∣Y=y]=2+3y3(2y+1)E[X\mid Y=y]=\dfrac{2+3y}{3(2y+1)}E[X∣Y=y]=3(2y+1)2+3y​, 0≤y≤10\le y\le10≤y≤1.

    • (d) The integral ∫01xfX∣Y(x∣y) dx\int_0^1 x f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\,dx∫01​xfX∣Y​(x∣y)dx set up (1) and simplified to 2+3y3(2y+1)\frac{2+3y}{3(2y+1)}3(2y+1)2+3y​ (1).

    MS26.3bcUniform on the triangle 0 < x < y < 1: f(x | y) and P(X < 1/2 | Y = 3/4) 2026 Midsem · Q3(b),(c) · 6 marks★ Must-do
    Let XXX and YYY have joint probability density function fX,Y(x,y)={2,0<x<y<1,0,otherwise.f_{X,Y}(x,y)=\begin{cases}2, & 0\lt x\lt y\lt 1,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}fX,Y​(x,y)={2,0,​0<x<y<1,otherwise.​ (b) Find the conditional PDF fX∣Y(x∣y)f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)fX∣Y​(x∣y). [3 marks]

    Same as: midsem sample bank SB.A16. (Part (a), the marginals, is in Topic 4.)

    Solution · follows the official key

    From part (a): for 0<y<10\lt y\lt10<y<1, fY(y)=∫0y2 dx=2yf_Y(y)=\int_0^y 2\,dx=2yfY​(y)=∫0y​2dx=2y, and fY(y)=0f_Y(y)=0fY​(y)=0 otherwise.

    (b)

    For y∈(0,1)y\in(0,1)y∈(0,1) (where fY(y)>0f_Y(y)\gt 0fY​(y)>0) and 0<x<y0\lt x\lt y0<x<y: fX∣Y(x∣y)=fX,Y(x,y)fY(y)=22y=1y,and fX∣Y(x∣y)=0 otherwise.f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}=\frac{2}{2y}=\frac1y,\qquad\text{and } f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=0 \text{ otherwise.}fX∣Y​(x∣y)=fY​(y)fX,Y​(x,y)​=2y2​=y1​,and fX∣Y​(x∣y)=0 otherwise. So given Y=yY=yY=y, X∼X\simX∼ Uniform(0,y)(0,y)(0,y).

    (c)

    Put y=34y=\frac34y=43​: fX∣Y(x∣34)=43f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid\frac34)=\frac{4}{3}fX∣Y​(x∣43​)=34​ for 0<x<340\lt x\lt\frac340<x<43​. Then P(X<12 | Y=34)=∫01/243 dx=43⋅12=23.P\left(X\lt\tfrac12\,\middle|\,Y=\tfrac34\right)=\int_0^{1/2}\frac43\,dx=\frac43\cdot\frac12=\frac23.P(X<21​​Y=43​)=∫01/2​34​dx=34​⋅21​=32​.

    Answer

    fX∣Y(x∣y)=1/yf_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1/yfX∣Y​(x∣y)=1/y on 0<x<y0\lt x\lt y0<x<y (Uniform(0,y)(0,y)(0,y)), 0<y<10\lt y\lt10<y<1; P(X<12∣Y=34)=23P(X\lt\frac12\mid Y=\frac34)=\frac23P(X<21​∣Y=43​)=32​.

    The joint density function is given as fX,Y(x,y)=cx(y−x)e−yf_{X,Y}(x,y)=cx(y-x)e^{-y}fX,Y​(x,y)=cx(y−x)e−y for 0≤x≤y<∞0\le x\le y\lt\infty0≤x≤y<∞.
    1. Find ccc.
    2. Show that: fX∣Y(x∣y)=6x(y−x)y3,0≤x≤y,fY∣X(y∣x)=(y−x)ex−y,0≤x≤y<∞.f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{6x(y-x)}{y^3},\quad 0\le x\le y,\qquad f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=(y-x)e^{x-y},\quad 0\le x\le y\lt\infty.fX∣Y​(x∣y)=y36x(y−x)​,0≤x≤y,fY∣X​(y∣x)=(y−x)ex−y,0≤x≤y<∞.

    Same as: 2025 HW 5 Q6 (H25-05.6, parts (a)–(b) only). Do it once.

    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    Support: {0≤x≤y}\{0\le x\le y\}{0≤x≤y}. For fixed y>0y\gt0y>0 the slice is 0≤x≤y0\le x\le y0≤x≤y; for fixed x≥0x\ge0x≥0 it is y≥xy\ge xy≥x.

    (a)

    1=c∫0∞e−y∫0yx(y−x) dx dy=c∫0∞e−y(y32−y33)dy=c6∫0∞y3e−y dy=c6⋅3!=c,1=c\int_0^\infty e^{-y}\int_0^y x(y-x)\,dx\,dy=c\int_0^\infty e^{-y}\Big(\frac{y^3}{2}-\frac{y^3}{3}\Big)dy=\frac c6\int_0^\infty y^3e^{-y}\,dy=\frac c6\cdot 3!=c,1=c∫0∞​e−y∫0y​x(y−x)dxdy=c∫0∞​e−y(2y3​−3y3​)dy=6c​∫0∞​y3e−ydy=6c​⋅3!=c, so c=1c=1c=1.

    (b)

    Marginals: for y≥0y\ge0y≥0, fY(y)=∫0yx(y−x)e−ydx=y3e−y6f_Y(y)=\int_0^y x(y-x)e^{-y}dx=\frac{y^3e^{-y}}{6}fY​(y)=∫0y​x(y−x)e−ydx=6y3e−y​. For x≥0x\ge0x≥0, substituting u=y−xu=y-xu=y−x, fX(x)=x∫x∞(y−x)e−y dy=xe−x∫0∞ue−u du=xe−x.f_X(x)=x\int_x^\infty (y-x)e^{-y}\,dy=xe^{-x}\int_0^\infty ue^{-u}\,du=xe^{-x}.fX​(x)=x∫x∞​(y−x)e−ydy=xe−x∫0∞​ue−udu=xe−x. Then, for y>0y\gt0y>0 and x>0x\gt0x>0 respectively, fX∣Y(x∣y)=x(y−x)e−yy3e−y/6=6x(y−x)y3, 0≤x≤y;fY∣X(y∣x)=x(y−x)e−yxe−x=(y−x)ex−y, y≥x,f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{x(y-x)e^{-y}}{y^3e^{-y}/6}=\frac{6x(y-x)}{y^3},\ 0\le x\le y;\qquad f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\frac{x(y-x)e^{-y}}{xe^{-x}}=(y-x)e^{x-y},\ y\ge x,fX∣Y​(x∣y)=y3e−y/6x(y−x)e−y​=y36x(y−x)​, 0≤x≤y;fY∣X​(y∣x)=xe−xx(y−x)e−y​=(y−x)ex−y, y≥x, and both are 0 off the slice, as required.

    (c)

    For y>0y\gt0y>0: E[X∣Y=y]=∫0yx⋅6x(y−x)y3 dx=6y3(y43−y44)=6y3⋅y412=y2.E[X\mid Y=y]=\int_0^y x\cdot\frac{6x(y-x)}{y^3}\,dx=\frac{6}{y^3}\Big(\frac{y^4}{3}-\frac{y^4}{4}\Big)=\frac{6}{y^3}\cdot\frac{y^4}{12}=\frac y2.E[X∣Y=y]=∫0y​x⋅y36x(y−x)​dx=y36​(3y4​−4y4​)=y36​⋅12y4​=2y​. Since this holds for every yyy, the random variable E[X∣Y]=g(Y)E[X\mid Y]=g(Y)E[X∣Y]=g(Y) with g(y)=y/2g(y)=y/2g(y)=y/2, i.e. E[X∣Y]=Y/2E[X\mid Y]=Y/2E[X∣Y]=Y/2. (Intuition: fX∣Yf_{X\mid Y}fX∣Y​ is symmetric about y/2y/2y/2 on [0,y][0,y][0,y].)

    Answer

    c=1c=1c=1; the two conditionals as stated; E[X∣Y]=Y/2E[X\mid Y]=Y/2E[X∣Y]=Y/2.

    T26-07.68xy on 0 < x < y < 1: marginals, conditionals, E[X] two ways 2026 Tut 7 Q6
    Let X,YX,YX,Y be jointly continuous random variables with joint density fX,Y(x,y)=8xy,0<x<y<1,f_{X,Y}(x,y)=8xy,\quad 0\lt x\lt y\lt 1,fX,Y​(x,y)=8xy,0<x<y<1, and fX,Y(x,y)=0f_{X,Y}(x,y)=0fX,Y​(x,y)=0 otherwise.
    1. Verify that this is a valid joint density.
    2. Find the marginal densities fX(x)f_X(x)fX​(x) and fY(y)f_Y(y)fY​(y).
    3. Find the conditional densities fX∣Y(x∣y)f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)fX∣Y​(x∣y) and fY∣X(y∣x)f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)fY∣X​(y∣x).
    4. Find E[X∣Y=y]\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=y]E[X∣Y=y] and E[Y∣X=x]\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]E[Y∣X=x].
    5. Use the law of iterated expectation to compute E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X], and verify your answer by computing E[X]\mathbb{E}[X]E[X] directly from fX(x)f_X(x)fX​(x).
    Solution · written for this guide

    (a)

    8xy≥08xy\ge08xy≥0 on the support and ∫01∫0y8xy dx dy=∫014y3 dy=1\int_0^1\int_0^y 8xy\,dx\,dy=\int_0^1 4y^3\,dy=1∫01​∫0y​8xydxdy=∫01​4y3dy=1. Valid.

    (b)

    For 0<x<10\lt x\lt10<x<1: fX(x)=∫x18xy dy=4x(1−x2)f_X(x)=\int_x^1 8xy\,dy=4x(1-x^2)fX​(x)=∫x1​8xydy=4x(1−x2). For 0<y<10\lt y\lt10<y<1: fY(y)=∫0y8xy dx=4y3f_Y(y)=\int_0^y8xy\,dx=4y^3fY​(y)=∫0y​8xydx=4y3. Both 0 outside (0,1)(0,1)(0,1).

    (c)

    For 0<y<10\lt y\lt10<y<1: fX∣Y(x∣y)=8xy4y3=2xy2f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\dfrac{8xy}{4y^3}=\dfrac{2x}{y^2}fX∣Y​(x∣y)=4y38xy​=y22x​, 0<x<y0\lt x\lt y0<x<y. For 0<x<10\lt x\lt10<x<1: fY∣X(y∣x)=8xy4x(1−x2)=2y1−x2f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\dfrac{8xy}{4x(1-x^2)}=\dfrac{2y}{1-x^2}fY∣X​(y∣x)=4x(1−x2)8xy​=1−x22y​, x<y<1x\lt y\lt1x<y<1. Both 0 off the slice.

    (d)

    E[X∣Y=y]=∫0yx2xy2dx=2y3,E[Y∣X=x]=∫x1y2y1−x2dy=2(1−x3)3(1−x2)=2(1+x+x2)3(1+x).E[X\mid Y=y]=\int_0^y x\frac{2x}{y^2}dx=\frac{2y}{3},\qquad E[Y\mid X=x]=\int_x^1 y\frac{2y}{1-x^2}dy=\frac{2(1-x^3)}{3(1-x^2)}=\frac{2(1+x+x^2)}{3(1+x)}.E[X∣Y=y]=∫0y​xy22x​dx=32y​,E[Y∣X=x]=∫x1​y1−x22y​dy=3(1−x2)2(1−x3)​=3(1+x)2(1+x+x2)​.

    (e)

    By (d), E[X∣Y]=23YE[X\mid Y]=\frac23YE[X∣Y]=32​Y. By the law of iterated expectation, E[X]=E[E[X∣Y]]=23E[Y]=23∫01y⋅4y3dy=23⋅45=815.E[X]=E\big[E[X\mid Y]\big]=\tfrac23E[Y]=\tfrac23\int_0^1 y\cdot4y^3dy=\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac45=\tfrac{8}{15}.E[X]=E[E[X∣Y]]=32​E[Y]=32​∫01​y⋅4y3dy=32​⋅54​=158​. Directly: E[X]=∫01x⋅4x(1−x2) dx=4(13−15)=815E[X]=\int_0^1 x\cdot4x(1-x^2)\,dx=4\big(\tfrac13-\tfrac15\big)=\tfrac{8}{15}E[X]=∫01​x⋅4x(1−x2)dx=4(31​−51​)=158​. They agree.

    Answer

    fX=4x(1−x2)f_X=4x(1-x^2)fX​=4x(1−x2), fY=4y3f_Y=4y^3fY​=4y3; fX∣Y=2x/y2f_{X\mid Y}=2x/y^2fX∣Y​=2x/y2 on (0,y)(0,y)(0,y), fY∣X=2y/(1−x2)f_{Y\mid X}=2y/(1-x^2)fY∣X​=2y/(1−x2) on (x,1)(x,1)(x,1); E[X∣Y=y]=2y/3E[X\mid Y=y]=2y/3E[X∣Y=y]=2y/3, E[Y∣X=x]=2(1+x+x2)3(1+x)E[Y\mid X=x]=\frac{2(1+x+x^2)}{3(1+x)}E[Y∣X=x]=3(1+x)2(1+x+x2)​; E[X]=8/15E[X]=8/15E[X]=8/15.

    H26-07.5E[X | Y = 2] and Var(X | Y = 2) for a polynomial density 2026 HW 7 Q5
    Let XXX and YYY be two jointly continuous random variables with joint probability density function (PDF) given by: fXY(x,y)={x26+y26+xy8,0≤x≤2, 0≤y≤30,otherwisef_{XY}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\frac{x^2}{6}+\frac{y^2}{6}+\frac{xy}{8}, & 0\le x\le 2,\ 0\le y\le 3\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}fXY​(x,y)={6x2​+6y2​+8xy​,0,​0≤x≤2, 0≤y≤3otherwise​ For 0≤y≤30\le y\le 30≤y≤3, find: E[X∣Y=2]\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y=2]E[X∣Y=2] and Var(X∣Y=2)\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y=2)Var(X∣Y=2).

    Related (different density): 2025 HW 5 Q9, H25-05.9.

    Solution · written for this guide
    The given function is not a PDF

    ∫03∫02(x26+y26+xy8)dx dy=43+3+98=13124≠1\int_0^3\int_0^2\big(\frac{x^2}{6}+\frac{y^2}{6}+\frac{xy}{8}\big)dx\,dy=\frac43+3+\frac98=\frac{131}{24}\ne1∫03​∫02​(6x2​+6y2​+8xy​)dxdy=34​+3+89​=24131​=1. The conditional density does not depend on the normalising constant (it cancels in fX,Y/fYf_{X,Y}/f_YfX,Y​/fY​), so the answers below are the same for the corrected density 24131(⋯ )\frac{24}{131}(\cdots)13124​(⋯). Say this in one line in an exam.

    Marginal (up to the same constant): for 0≤y≤30\le y\le30≤y≤3, fY(y)=∫02(x26+y26+xy8)dx=49+y23+y4,fY(2)=49+43+12=4118.f_Y(y)=\int_0^2\Big(\frac{x^2}{6}+\frac{y^2}{6}+\frac{xy}{8}\Big)dx=\frac49+\frac{y^2}{3}+\frac y4,\qquad f_Y(2)=\frac49+\frac43+\frac12=\frac{41}{18}.fY​(y)=∫02​(6x2​+6y2​+8xy​)dx=94​+3y2​+4y​,fY​(2)=94​+34​+21​=1841​. Conditional density at y=2y=2y=2, for 0≤x≤20\le x\le 20≤x≤2: fX∣Y(x∣2)=x26+23+x441/18=6x2+9x+2482(0 otherwise).f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid 2)=\frac{\frac{x^2}{6}+\frac23+\frac x4}{41/18}=\frac{6x^2+9x+24}{82}\quad(\text{0 otherwise}).fX∣Y​(x∣2)=41/186x2​+32​+4x​​=826x2+9x+24​(0 otherwise). Moments: E[X∣Y=2]=182∫02(6x3+9x2+24x) dx=24+24+4882=4841,E[X\mid Y=2]=\frac{1}{82}\int_0^2(6x^3+9x^2+24x)\,dx=\frac{24+24+48}{82}=\frac{48}{41},E[X∣Y=2]=821​∫02​(6x3+9x2+24x)dx=8224+24+48​=4148​, E[X2∣Y=2]=182∫02(6x4+9x3+24x2) dx=1925+36+6482=346205,E[X^2\mid Y=2]=\frac{1}{82}\int_0^2(6x^4+9x^3+24x^2)\,dx=\frac{\frac{192}{5}+36+64}{82}=\frac{346}{205},E[X2∣Y=2]=821​∫02​(6x4+9x3+24x2)dx=825192​+36+64​=205346​, Var(X∣Y=2)=346205−(4841)2=14186−115208405=26668405.\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y=2)=\frac{346}{205}-\Big(\frac{48}{41}\Big)^2=\frac{14186-11520}{8405}=\frac{2666}{8405}.Var(X∣Y=2)=205346​−(4148​)2=840514186−11520​=84052666​.

    Let XXX and YYY be two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF fX,Y(x,y)={x24+y24+xy6,0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤2,0,otherwise.f_{X,Y}(x,y)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x^2}{4}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}+\dfrac{xy}{6}, & 0\le x\le 1,\ 0\le y\le 2,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}fX,Y​(x,y)=⎩⎨⎧​4x2​+4y2​+6xy​,0,​0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤2,otherwise.​ For 0≤y≤20\le y\le 20≤y≤2, find
    1. the conditional PDF of XXX given Y=yY=yY=y.

    (This one is a valid PDF: ∫02(112+y24+y12)dy=16+23+16=1\int_0^2\big(\frac1{12}+\frac{y^2}{4}+\frac y{12}\big)dy=\frac16+\frac23+\frac16=1∫02​(121​+4y2​+12y​)dy=61​+32​+61​=1.)

So for 0≤y≤20\le y\le20≤y≤2: fX∣Y(x∣y)=fX,Y(x,y)fY(y)={3x2+3y2+2xy3y2+y+1,0≤x≤1,0,otherwise.f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{X,Y}(x,y)}{f_Y(y)}=\begin{cases}\dfrac{3x^2+3y^2+2xy}{3y^2+y+1}, & 0\le x\le1,\\[4pt] 0, &\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}fX∣Y​(x∣y)=fY​(y)fX,Y​(x,y)​=⎩⎨⎧​3y2+y+13x2+3y2+2xy​,0,​0≤x≤1,otherwise.​

    T26-07.7Entropy, conditional entropy and mutual information 2026 Tut 7 Q7
    Let XXX and YYY be discrete random variables with joint PMF pX,Y(x,y)p_{X,Y}(x,y)pX,Y​(x,y). Entropy of XXX is H(X)=−∑xpX(x)log⁡2pX(x)=E[−log⁡2pX(X)].H(X)=-\sum_x p_X(x)\log_2 p_X(x)=\mathbb{E}\left[-\log_2 p_X(X)\right].H(X)=−x∑​pX​(x)log2​pX​(x)=E[−log2​pX​(X)]. We define the following quantities (all logarithms are base 2, all sums run over values with non-zero probability, and we use the convention 0log⁡20=00\log_2 0=00log2​0=0):
    • Joint entropy: H(X,Y)=−∑x∑ypX,Y(x,y)log⁡2pX,Y(x,y)H(X,Y)=-\sum_x\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log_2 p_{X,Y}(x,y)H(X,Y)=−∑x​∑y​pX,Y​(x,y)log2​pX,Y​(x,y).
    • Conditional entropy of XXX given Y=yY=yY=y: the entropy of the conditional PMF of XXX given Y=yY=yY=y, H(X∣Y=y)=−∑xpX∣Y(x∣y)log⁡2pX∣Y(x∣y)H(X\mid Y=y)=-\sum_x p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\log_2 p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)H(X∣Y=y)=−∑x​pX∣Y​(x∣y)log2​pX∣Y​(x∣y).
    • Conditional entropy of XXX given YYY: H(X∣Y)=∑ypY(y) H(X∣Y=y)H(X\mid Y)=\sum_y p_Y(y)\,H(X\mid Y=y)H(X∣Y)=∑y​pY​(y)H(X∣Y=y).
    • Mutual information of XXX and YYY: H(X)−H(X∣Y)H(X)-H(X\mid Y)H(X)−H(X∣Y).
    1. Show that H(X∣Y)=E[−log⁡2pX∣Y(X∣Y)]=−∑x∑ypX,Y(x,y)log⁡2pX∣Y(x∣y)H(X\mid Y)=\mathbb{E}\left[-\log_2 p_{X\mid Y}(X\mid Y)\right]=-\sum_x\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log_2 p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)H(X∣Y)=E[−log2​pX∣Y​(X∣Y)]=−∑x​∑y​pX,Y​(x,y)log2​pX∣Y​(x∣y).
    2. Show that H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=H(X)−H(X∣Y)H(Y)-H(Y\mid X)=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=H(X)−H(X∣Y).
    3. Show the chain rule H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y)H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X\mid Y)H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y). Hence deduce that H(X)−H(X∣Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y)H(X)-H(X\mid Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)H(X)−H(X∣Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y).
    4. Show that if XXX and YYY are independent, then their mutual information is 0, i.e. H(X)−H(X∣Y)=0H(X)-H(X\mid Y)=0H(X)−H(X∣Y)=0.
    Solution · written for this guide

    Write log⁡\loglog for log⁡2\log_2log2​. Everything rests on pX,Y(x,y)=pY(y)pX∣Y(x∣y)=pX(x)pY∣X(y∣x)p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_Y(y)p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=p_X(x)p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)pX,Y​(x,y)=pY​(y)pX∣Y​(x∣y)=pX​(x)pY∣X​(y∣x) and on LOTUS for a function of two variables, E[g(X,Y)]=∑x∑yg(x,y)pX,Y(x,y)E[g(X,Y)]=\sum_x\sum_y g(x,y)p_{X,Y}(x,y)E[g(X,Y)]=∑x​∑y​g(x,y)pX,Y​(x,y).

    (a)

    H(X∣Y)=∑ypY(y)(−∑xpX∣Y(x∣y)log⁡pX∣Y(x∣y))=−∑x∑ypY(y)pX∣Y(x∣y)⏟=pX,Y(x,y)log⁡pX∣Y(x∣y).H(X\mid Y)=\sum_y p_Y(y)\Big(-\sum_x p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\log p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)\Big)=-\sum_x\sum_y \underbrace{p_Y(y)p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)}_{=p_{X,Y}(x,y)}\log p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y).H(X∣Y)=y∑​pY​(y)(−x∑​pX∣Y​(x∣y)logpX∣Y​(x∣y))=−x∑​y∑​=pX,Y​(x,y)pY​(y)pX∣Y​(x∣y)​​logpX∣Y​(x∣y). By LOTUS with g(x,y)=−log⁡pX∣Y(x∣y)g(x,y)=-\log p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)g(x,y)=−logpX∣Y​(x∣y), this double sum is E[−log⁡pX∣Y(X∣Y)]E\big[-\log p_{X\mid Y}(X\mid Y)\big]E[−logpX∣Y​(X∣Y)]. (Only pairs with pX,Y>0p_{X,Y}\gt0pX,Y​>0 appear, so every log is finite.)

    (c) Chain rule (done before (b) because (b) follows from it)

    Taking logs of pX,Y=pY pX∣Yp_{X,Y}=p_Y\,p_{X\mid Y}pX,Y​=pY​pX∣Y​ gives −log⁡pX,Y(x,y)=−log⁡pY(y)−log⁡pX∣Y(x∣y)-\log p_{X,Y}(x,y)=-\log p_Y(y)-\log p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)−logpX,Y​(x,y)=−logpY​(y)−logpX∣Y​(x∣y). Multiply by pX,Y(x,y)p_{X,Y}(x,y)pX,Y​(x,y) and sum over x,yx,yx,y: H(X,Y)=−∑y(∑xpX,Y(x,y))log⁡pY(y)+H(X∣Y)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y),H(X,Y)=-\sum_y\Big(\sum_x p_{X,Y}(x,y)\Big)\log p_Y(y)+H(X\mid Y)=H(Y)+H(X\mid Y),H(X,Y)=−y∑​(x∑​pX,Y​(x,y))logpY​(y)+H(X∣Y)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y), using ∑xpX,Y(x,y)=pY(y)\sum_x p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_Y(y)∑x​pX,Y​(x,y)=pY​(y) and part (a). Hence H(X∣Y)=H(X,Y)−H(Y)H(X\mid Y)=H(X,Y)-H(Y)H(X∣Y)=H(X,Y)−H(Y) and H(X)−H(X∣Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y).H(X)-H(X\mid Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y).H(X)−H(X∣Y)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y).

    (b)

    The same argument with the roles of XXX and YYY swapped (pX,Y=pX pY∣Xp_{X,Y}=p_X\,p_{Y\mid X}pX,Y​=pX​pY∣X​) gives H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y∣X)H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y\mid X)H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y∣X), so H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y)H(Y)-H(Y\mid X)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)H(Y)−H(Y∣X)=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y). The right-hand side is symmetric in XXX and YYY, so it equals H(X)−H(X∣Y)H(X)-H(X\mid Y)H(X)−H(X∣Y) from (c).

    (d)

    If X,YX,YX,Y are independent then pX∣Y(x∣y)=pX(x)p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=p_X(x)pX∣Y​(x∣y)=pX​(x) for every yyy with pY(y)>0p_Y(y)\gt0pY​(y)>0. So H(X∣Y=y)=H(X)H(X\mid Y=y)=H(X)H(X∣Y=y)=H(X) for each such yyy, and H(X∣Y)=∑ypY(y)H(X)=H(X)H(X\mid Y)=\sum_y p_Y(y)H(X)=H(X)H(X∣Y)=∑y​pY​(y)H(X)=H(X). The mutual information is H(X)−H(X)=0H(X)-H(X)=0H(X)−H(X)=0.

    Answer

    H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y)=H(X)+H(Y∣X)H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X\mid Y)=H(X)+H(Y\mid X)H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X∣Y)=H(X)+H(Y∣X), so the mutual information H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y)H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y) is symmetric, and it is 0 under independence.

    PCS5.2.5.46xy on 0 ≤ y ≤ √x: conditional mean and variance PC §5.2.5 Solved Problem 4
    Let XXX and YYY be two jointly continuous random variables with joint PDF fX,Y(x,y)={6xy,0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤x,0,otherwise.f_{X,Y}(x,y)=\begin{cases}6xy, & 0\le x\le1,\ 0\le y\le\sqrt x,\\ 0, &\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}fX,Y​(x,y)={6xy,0,​0≤x≤1, 0≤y≤x​,otherwise.​
    1. Show RXYR_{XY}RXY​ in the xxx-yyy plane.
    2. Find fX(x)f_X(x)fX​(x) and fY(y)f_Y(y)fY​(y).
    3. Are XXX and YYY independent?
    4. Find the conditional PDF of XXX given Y=yY=yY=y, fX∣Y(x∣y)f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)fX∣Y​(x∣y).
    5. Find E[X∣Y=y]E[X\mid Y=y]E[X∣Y=y], for 0≤y≤10\le y\le10≤y≤1.
    6. Find Var(X∣Y=y)\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y=y)Var(X∣Y=y), for 0≤y≤10\le y\le 10≤y≤1.
    Solution · follows ProbabilityCourse's solution

    (a)

    RXYR_{XY}RXY​ is the region of the unit square under the curve y=xy=\sqrt xy=x​ (equivalently y2≤x≤1y^2\le x\le1y2≤x≤1, 0≤y≤10\le y\le10≤y≤1). For fixed yyy the slice is x∈[y2,1]x\in[y^2,1]x∈[y2,1]; for fixed xxx it is y∈[0,x]y\in[0,\sqrt x]y∈[0,x​].

    (b)

    fX(x)=∫0x6xy dy=3x2f_X(x)=\int_0^{\sqrt x}6xy\,dy=3x^2fX​(x)=∫0x​​6xydy=3x2 for 0≤x≤10\le x\le10≤x≤1; fY(y)=∫y216xy dx=3y(1−y4)f_Y(y)=\int_{y^2}^1 6xy\,dx=3y(1-y^4)fY​(y)=∫y21​6xydx=3y(1−y4) for 0≤y≤10\le y\le10≤y≤1.

    (c)

    No: fX(x)fY(y)=9x2y(1−y4)≠6xyf_X(x)f_Y(y)=9x^2y(1-y^4)\ne 6xyfX​(x)fY​(y)=9x2y(1−y4)=6xy; also RXYR_{XY}RXY​ is not a rectangle.

    (d)

    For 0≤y<10\le y\lt10≤y<1: fX∣Y(x∣y)=6xy3y(1−y4)=2x1−y4f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\dfrac{6xy}{3y(1-y^4)}=\dfrac{2x}{1-y^4}fX∣Y​(x∣y)=3y(1−y4)6xy​=1−y42x​ for y2≤x≤1y^2\le x\le1y2≤x≤1, 0 otherwise.

    (e)

    E[X∣Y=y]=∫y212x21−y4dx=2(1−y6)3(1−y4)=2(1+y2+y4)3(1+y2).E[X\mid Y=y]=\int_{y^2}^1\frac{2x^2}{1-y^4}dx=\frac{2(1-y^6)}{3(1-y^4)}=\frac{2(1+y^2+y^4)}{3(1+y^2)}.E[X∣Y=y]=∫y21​1−y42x2​dx=3(1−y4)2(1−y6)​=3(1+y2)2(1+y2+y4)​.

    (f)

    E[X2∣Y=y]=∫y212x31−y4dx=1−y82(1−y4)=1+y42E[X^2\mid Y=y]=\int_{y^2}^1\frac{2x^3}{1-y^4}dx=\frac{1-y^8}{2(1-y^4)}=\frac{1+y^4}{2}E[X2∣Y=y]=∫y21​1−y42x3​dx=2(1−y4)1−y8​=21+y4​, so Var(X∣Y=y)=1+y42−4(1+y2+y4)29(1+y2)2=(1−y2)2(1+4y2+y4)18(1+y2)2.\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y=y)=\frac{1+y^4}{2}-\frac{4(1+y^2+y^4)^2}{9(1+y^2)^2}=\frac{(1-y^2)^2(1+4y^2+y^4)}{18(1+y^2)^2}.Var(X∣Y=y)=21+y4​−9(1+y2)24(1+y2+y4)2​=18(1+y2)2(1−y2)2(1+4y2+y4)​.

    Answer

    fX=3x2f_X=3x^2fX​=3x2, fY=3y(1−y4)f_Y=3y(1-y^4)fY​=3y(1−y4), not independent, fX∣Y=2x1−y4f_{X\mid Y}=\frac{2x}{1-y^4}fX∣Y​=1−y42x​ on [y2,1][y^2,1][y2,1]; E[X∣Y=y]=2(1−y6)3(1−y4)E[X\mid Y=y]=\frac{2(1-y^6)}{3(1-y^4)}E[X∣Y=y]=3(1−y4)2(1−y6)​, Var(X∣Y=y)=1+y42−(2(1−y6)3(1−y4))2\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y=y)=\frac{1+y^4}{2}-\Big(\frac{2(1-y^6)}{3(1-y^4)}\Big)^2Var(X∣Y=y)=21+y4​−(3(1−y4)2(1−y6)​)2.

    PC5.4.23Uniform on the diamond |x| + |y| ≤ 1 PC §5.4 Problem 23
    Consider the set E={(x,y)∣∣x∣+∣y∣≤1}E=\{(x,y)\mid |x|+|y|\le1\}E={(x,y)∣∣x∣+∣y∣≤1}. Suppose that we choose a point (X,Y)(X,Y)(X,Y) uniformly at random in EEE. That is, the joint PDF of XXX and YYY is given by fXY(x,y)={c,(x,y)∈E,0,otherwise.f_{XY}(x,y)=\begin{cases}c, & (x,y)\in E,\\ 0, &\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}fXY​(x,y)={c,0,​(x,y)∈E,otherwise.​
    1. Find the constant ccc.

    BT3.23Uniform on a triangle: E[X] by total expectation and symmetry B&T Ch. 3 Problem 23
    Let the random variables XXX and YYY have a joint PDF which is uniform over the triangle with vertices at (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), and (1,0)(1,0)(1,0).
    1. Find the joint PDF of XXX and YYY.
    2. Find the marginal PDF of YYY.
    3. Find the conditional PDF of XXX given YYY.
    4. Find E[X∣Y=y]E[X\mid Y=y]E[X∣Y=y], and use the total expectation theorem to find E[X]E[X]E[X] in terms of E[Y]E[Y]E[Y].
    5. Use the symmetry of the problem to find the value of E[X]E[X]E[X].
    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    (a)

    The triangle {x≥0, y≥0, x+y≤1}\{x\ge0,\ y\ge0,\ x+y\le1\}{x≥0, y≥0, x+y≤1} has area 12\frac1221​, so fX,Y(x,y)=2f_{X,Y}(x,y)=2fX,Y​(x,y)=2 on it and 0 elsewhere.

    (b)

    fY(y)=∫01−y2 dx=2(1−y)f_Y(y)=\int_0^{1-y}2\,dx=2(1-y)fY​(y)=∫01−y​2dx=2(1−y), 0≤y≤10\le y\le10≤y≤1.

    (c)

    For 0≤y<10\le y\lt10≤y<1: fX∣Y(x∣y)=22(1−y)=11−yf_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\dfrac{2}{2(1-y)}=\dfrac1{1-y}fX∣Y​(x∣y)=2(1−y)2​=1−y1​, 0≤x≤1−y0\le x\le1-y0≤x≤1−y: Uniform[0,1−y][0,1-y][0,1−y]. Undefined for y∉[0,1)y\notin[0,1)y∈/[0,1) (where fY=0f_Y=0fY​=0).

    (d)

    The mean of Uniform[0,1−y][0,1-y][0,1−y]: E[X∣Y=y]=1−y2E[X\mid Y=y]=\frac{1-y}{2}E[X∣Y=y]=21−y​, 0≤y≤10\le y\le10≤y≤1. Total expectation theorem: E[X]=∫01E[X∣Y=y]fY(y) dy=∫011−y2fY(y) dy=12−12∫01yfY(y) dy=1−E[Y]2.E[X]=\int_0^1E[X\mid Y=y]f_Y(y)\,dy=\int_0^1\frac{1-y}{2}f_Y(y)\,dy=\frac12-\frac12\int_0^1 yf_Y(y)\,dy=\frac{1-E[Y]}{2}.E[X]=∫01​E[X∣Y=y]fY​(y)dy=∫01​21−y​fY​(y)dy=21​−21​∫01​yfY​(y)dy=21−E[Y]​.

    (e)

    The triangle is symmetric under (x,y)↦(y,x)(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)(x,y)↦(y,x), so XXX and YYY have the same distribution and E[X]=E[Y]E[X]=E[Y]E[X]=E[Y]. Then E[X]=1−E[X]2E[X]=\frac{1-E[X]}{2}E[X]=21−E[X]​, so E[X]=13E[X]=\frac13E[X]=31​.

    Answer

    fX,Y=2f_{X,Y}=2fX,Y​=2; fY=2(1−y)f_Y=2(1-y)fY​=2(1−y); X∣Y=y∼U[0,1−y]X\mid Y=y\sim U[0,1-y]X∣Y=y∼U[0,1−y]; E[X]=1−E[Y]2E[X]=\frac{1-E[Y]}{2}E[X]=21−E[Y]​; E[X]=1/3E[X]=1/3E[X]=1/3.

    Official solution: B&T solutions, pp. 43–44.

    3  E[X | Y] as a random variable and the law of iterated expectation · Lecture 12

    Theory recap

    For each value yyy, E[X∣Y=y]E[X\mid Y=y]E[X∣Y=y] is a number g(y)g(y)g(y). Plugging in the random YYY gives the random variable E[X∣Y]=g(Y)E[X\mid Y]=g(Y)E[X∣Y]=g(Y): a function of YYY only, taking the value g(y)g(y)g(y) with probability pY(y)p_Y(y)pY​(y) (or with density fYf_YfY​).

    Law of iterated expectation (total expectation theorem)

    E[E[X∣Y]]=E[X]:∑ypY(y) E[X∣Y=y]=E[X],∫fY(y) E[X∣Y=y] dy=E[X].E\big[E[X\mid Y]\big]=E[X]:\qquad \sum_y p_Y(y)\,E[X\mid Y=y]=E[X],\qquad \int f_Y(y)\,E[X\mid Y=y]\,dy=E[X].E[E[X∣Y]]=E[X]:y∑​pY​(y)E[X∣Y=y]=E[X],∫fY​(y)E[X∣Y=y]dy=E[X]. Proof (discrete): ∑ypY(y)∑xx pX∣Y(x∣y)=∑xx∑ypX,Y(x,y)=∑xx pX(x)\sum_y p_Y(y)\sum_x x\,p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\sum_x x\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)=\sum_x x\,p_X(x)∑y​pY​(y)∑x​xpX∣Y​(x∣y)=∑x​x∑y​pX,Y​(x,y)=∑x​xpX​(x). The same works with more conditioning variables (tower property): E[E[Z∣X,Y]∣X]=E[Z∣X]E\big[E[Z\mid X,Y]\mid X\big]=E[Z\mid X]E[E[Z∣X,Y]∣X]=E[Z∣X].

    Rules for computing E[ · | Y]
    • Linearity: E[aX+bZ∣Y]=aE[X∣Y]+bE[Z∣Y]E[aX+bZ\mid Y]=aE[X\mid Y]+bE[Z\mid Y]E[aX+bZ∣Y]=aE[X∣Y]+bE[Z∣Y].
    • Taking out what is known: E[g(Y)X∣Y]=g(Y)E[X∣Y]E[g(Y)X\mid Y]=g(Y)E[X\mid Y]E[g(Y)X∣Y]=g(Y)E[X∣Y]; in particular E[g(Y)∣Y]=g(Y)E[g(Y)\mid Y]=g(Y)E[g(Y)∣Y]=g(Y).
    • Independence: if XXX is independent of YYY, E[X∣Y]=E[X]E[X\mid Y]=E[X]E[X∣Y]=E[X] (a constant).
    • Write the answer as a function of the random YYY (e.g. E[X∣Y]=Y/2E[X\mid Y]=Y/2E[X∣Y]=Y/2), then take EEE of it.
    First-step analysis (recursions by conditioning)

    For "expected number of steps until …": let m(s)m(s)m(s) be the expected remaining steps from state sss. Condition on the first step S1S_1S1​: m(s)=1+E[m(S1)∣start at s]=1+∑s′P(s→s′) m(s′),m(s)=1+E\big[m(S_1)\mid \text{start at } s\big]=1+\sum_{s'}P(s\to s')\,m(s'),m(s)=1+E[m(S1​)∣start at s]=1+s′∑​P(s→s′)m(s′), with m=0m=0m=0 in the stopping states. This is the total expectation theorem over the partition {S1=s′}\{S_1=s'\}{S1​=s′}; it is valid because, given the first step, the future behaves like a fresh start from s′s's′ (independence of the steps). Solve the linear equations (or the integral equation for continuous steps).

    Watch out

    E[X∣Y]E[X\mid Y]E[X∣Y] is a random variable, E[X∣Y=y]E[X\mid Y=y]E[X∣Y=y] is a number, E[X]E[X]E[X] is a number. Graders look for the line "E[X∣Y]=…E[X\mid Y]=\dotsE[X∣Y]=… (a function of YYY), hence E[X]=E[E[X∣Y]]=…E[X]=E[E[X\mid Y]]=\dotsE[X]=E[E[X∣Y]]=…". When you write "given the first toss is T, it is like starting over", say why: the tosses are independent.

    Tutorials and homeworks

    T26-07.2Prove the tower property for three discrete variables 2026 Tut 7 Q2
    Let XXX, YYY, and ZZZ be discrete random variables. Show the following generalizations of the law of iterated expectations.
    1. E[Z]=E[E[Z∣X,Y]]\mathbb{E}[Z]=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[Z\mid X,Y]\right]E[Z]=E[E[Z∣X,Y]].
    2. E[Z∣X]=E[E[Z∣X,Y]∣X]\mathbb{E}[Z\mid X]=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{E}[Z\mid X,Y]\mid X\right]E[Z∣X]=E[E[Z∣X,Y]∣X].
    Solution · written for this guide

    Notation: p(x,y,z)=P(X=x,Y=y,Z=z)p(x,y,z)=P(X=x,Y=y,Z=z)p(x,y,z)=P(X=x,Y=y,Z=z), and for pX,Y(x,y)>0p_{X,Y}(x,y)\gt0pX,Y​(x,y)>0, pZ∣X,Y(z∣x,y)=p(x,y,z)/pX,Y(x,y)p_{Z\mid X,Y}(z\mid x,y)=p(x,y,z)/p_{X,Y}(x,y)pZ∣X,Y​(z∣x,y)=p(x,y,z)/pX,Y​(x,y). Let h(x,y)=E[Z∣X=x,Y=y]=∑zz pZ∣X,Y(z∣x,y)h(x,y)=E[Z\mid X=x,Y=y]=\sum_z z\,p_{Z\mid X,Y}(z\mid x,y)h(x,y)=E[Z∣X=x,Y=y]=∑z​zpZ∣X,Y​(z∣x,y), so E[Z∣X,Y]=h(X,Y)E[Z\mid X,Y]=h(X,Y)E[Z∣X,Y]=h(X,Y). (Assume E∣Z∣<∞E|Z|\lt\inftyE∣Z∣<∞ so all sums may be rearranged.)

    (a)

    By LOTUS for the function hhh of (X,Y)(X,Y)(X,Y): E[h(X,Y)]=∑x,ypX,Y(x,y)∑zzp(x,y,z)pX,Y(x,y)=∑zz∑x,yp(x,y,z)=∑zz pZ(z)=E[Z].E\big[h(X,Y)\big]=\sum_{x,y}p_{X,Y}(x,y)\sum_z z\frac{p(x,y,z)}{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}=\sum_z z\sum_{x,y}p(x,y,z)=\sum_z z\,p_Z(z)=E[Z].E[h(X,Y)]=x,y∑​pX,Y​(x,y)z∑​zpX,Y​(x,y)p(x,y,z)​=z∑​zx,y∑​p(x,y,z)=z∑​zpZ​(z)=E[Z].

    (b)

    Fix xxx with pX(x)>0p_X(x)\gt0pX​(x)>0. Conditional LOTUS (the YYY-average given X=xX=xX=x) gives E[h(X,Y)∣X=x]=∑yh(x,y) pY∣X(y∣x)=∑ypX,Y(x,y)pX(x)∑zzp(x,y,z)pX,Y(x,y)=∑zz∑yp(x,y,z)pX(x)=∑zz pZ∣X(z∣x),E\big[h(X,Y)\mid X=x\big]=\sum_y h(x,y)\,p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=\sum_y\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_X(x)}\sum_z z\frac{p(x,y,z)}{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}=\sum_z z\frac{\sum_y p(x,y,z)}{p_X(x)}=\sum_z z\,p_{Z\mid X}(z\mid x),E[h(X,Y)∣X=x]=y∑​h(x,y)pY∣X​(y∣x)=y∑​pX​(x)pX,Y​(x,y)​z∑​zpX,Y​(x,y)p(x,y,z)​=z∑​zpX​(x)∑y​p(x,y,z)​=z∑​zpZ∣X​(z∣x), which is E[Z∣X=x]E[Z\mid X=x]E[Z∣X=x]. The two functions of xxx agree at every xxx with pX(x)>0p_X(x)\gt0pX​(x)>0, so the random variables E[E[Z∣X,Y]∣X]E[E[Z\mid X,Y]\mid X]E[E[Z∣X,Y]∣X] and E[Z∣X]E[Z\mid X]E[Z∣X] are equal.

    Answer

    E[E[Z∣X,Y]]=E[Z]E[E[Z\mid X,Y]]=E[Z]E[E[Z∣X,Y]]=E[Z] and E[E[Z∣X,Y]∣X]=E[Z∣X]E[E[Z\mid X,Y]\mid X]=E[Z\mid X]E[E[Z∣X,Y]∣X]=E[Z∣X]: averaging over the extra information YYY gives back the coarser conditional expectation. (a) is (b) with no XXX.

    Case 0≤s<10\le s\lt10≤s<1

    Differentiating E(s)=1+∫ss+1E(t) dtE(s)=1+\int_s^{s+1}E(t)\,dtE(s)=1+∫ss+1​E(t)dt: E′(s)=E(s+1)−E(s)=e1−s−E(s)E'(s)=E(s+1)-E(s)=e^{1-s}-E(s)E′(s)=E(s+1)−E(s)=e1−s−E(s), since s+1∈[1,2)s+1\in[1,2)s+1∈[1,2). With the integrating factor ese^ses: dds(esE(s))=es(E′(s)+E(s))=e⟹esE(s)=es+K⟹E(s)=(es+K)e−s.\frac{d}{ds}\big(e^sE(s)\big)=e^s\big(E'(s)+E(s)\big)=e\quad\Longrightarrow\quad e^sE(s)=es+K\quad\Longrightarrow\quad E(s)=(es+K)e^{-s}.dsd​(esE(s))=es(E′(s)+E(s))=e⟹esE(s)=es+K⟹E(s)=(es+K)e−s. Hence E(0)=K=e2−e≈4.671.E(0)=K=e^2-e\approx4.671.E(0)=K=e2−e≈4.671. (Monte Carlo with 2×1052\times10^52×105 runs gives 4.6694.6694.669.)

    PCS5.1.6.6Expected tosses until two consecutive heads PC §5.1.6 Solved Problem 6
    I have a coin with P(H)=pP(H)=pP(H)=p. I toss the coin repeatedly until I observe two consecutive heads. Let XXX be the total number of coin tosses. Find EXEXEX.
    Solution · follows ProbabilityCourse's solution

    Let μ=EX\mu=EXμ=EX. Condition on the first toss: μ=E[X∣H]p+E[X∣T](1−p),E[X∣T]=1+μ,\mu=E[X\mid H]p+E[X\mid T](1-p),\qquad E[X\mid T]=1+\mu,μ=E[X∣H]p+E[X∣T](1−p),E[X∣T]=1+μ, because after a first tail the tosses are independent and the game starts over. To find E[X∣H]E[X\mid H]E[X∣H], condition on the second toss: E[X∣HH]=2E[X\mid HH]=2E[X∣HH]=2 (done), and E[X∣HT]=2+μE[X\mid HT]=2+\muE[X∣HT]=2+μ (two tosses used, then a fresh start). So E[X∣H]=2p+(2+μ)(1−p).E[X\mid H]=2p+(2+\mu)(1-p).E[X∣H]=2p+(2+μ)(1−p). Substituting, μ=p[2p+(2+μ)(1−p)]+(1−p)(1+μ)  ⟹  μ[1−p(1−p)−(1−p)]=1+p  ⟹  μp2=1+p.\mu=p\big[2p+(2+\mu)(1-p)\big]+(1-p)(1+\mu)\;\Longrightarrow\;\mu\big[1-p(1-p)-(1-p)\big]=1+p\;\Longrightarrow\;\mu p^2=1+p.μ=p[2p+(2+μ)(1−p)]+(1−p)(1+μ)⟹μ[1−p(1−p)−(1−p)]=1+p⟹μp2=1+p.

    Answer

    EX=1+pp2EX=\dfrac{1+p}{p^2}EX=p21+p​ (6 for a fair coin).

    4  Mixtures, random sums and the law of total variance · Lecture 12, Tut 7

    Theory recap

    Three standard models are solved by "condition on the hidden variable, then average": a mixture (pick a component at random, then sample from it), a random sum T=X1+⋯+XNT=X_1+\dots+X_NT=X1​+⋯+XN​, and a variable whose parameter is itself random. The mean comes from the law of iterated expectation; the variance from the law of total variance.

    Mixtures

    If P(Z=i)=piP(Z=i)=p_iP(Z=i)=pi​ and, given Z=iZ=iZ=i, XXX has the law of YiY_iYi​ (e.g. X=YZX=Y_ZX=YZ​ with ZZZ independent of the YiY_iYi​), then by total probability and total expectation FX(x)=∑ipiFYi(x),fX(x)=∑ipifYi(x),E[g(X)]=∑ipiE[g(Yi)].F_X(x)=\sum_i p_iF_{Y_i}(x),\qquad f_X(x)=\sum_i p_if_{Y_i}(x),\qquad E[g(X)]=\sum_i p_iE[g(Y_i)].FX​(x)=i∑​pi​FYi​​(x),fX​(x)=i∑​pi​fYi​​(x),E[g(X)]=i∑​pi​E[g(Yi​)]. Lecture example: X∼X\simX∼ Exp(Y)(Y)(Y) with Y=λ1Y=\lambda_1Y=λ1​ w.p. ppp, λ2\lambda_2λ2​ w.p. 1−p1-p1−p: E[X]=pλ1+1−pλ2E[X]=\frac p{\lambda_1}+\frac{1-p}{\lambda_2}E[X]=λ1​p​+λ2​1−p​.

    Law of total variance

    Var(X)=E[Var(X∣Y)]+Var(E[X∣Y]),\mathrm{Var}(X)=E\big[\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)\big]+\mathrm{Var}\big(E[X\mid Y]\big),Var(X)=E[Var(X∣Y)]+Var(E[X∣Y]), where Var(X∣Y)=E[X2∣Y]−(E[X∣Y])2\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)=E[X^2\mid Y]-(E[X\mid Y])^2Var(X∣Y)=E[X2∣Y]−(E[X∣Y])2 is a random variable (a function of YYY). "Average spread within groups + spread of the group means." Alternative: compute E[X2]=E[E[X2∣Y]]E[X^2]=E[E[X^2\mid Y]]E[X2]=E[E[X2∣Y]] and subtract (E[X])2(E[X])^2(E[X])2.

    Random sums

    T=∑i=1NXiT=\sum_{i=1}^N X_iT=∑i=1N​Xi​, with XiX_iXi​ i.i.d. (mean E[X]E[X]E[X], variance Var(X)\mathrm{Var}(X)Var(X)) and NNN a nonnegative integer RV independent of the XiX_iXi​. Given N=nN=nN=n, TTT is a fixed sum of nnn terms, so E[T∣N]=N E[X],Var(T∣N)=N Var(X),E[T\mid N]=N\,E[X],\qquad \mathrm{Var}(T\mid N)=N\,\mathrm{Var}(X),E[T∣N]=NE[X],Var(T∣N)=NVar(X), E[T]=E[N]E[X],Var(T)=E[N]Var(X)+(E[X])2Var(N).E[T]=E[N]E[X],\qquad \mathrm{Var}(T)=E[N]\mathrm{Var}(X)+(E[X])^2\mathrm{Var}(N).E[T]=E[N]E[X],Var(T)=E[N]Var(X)+(E[X])2Var(N). (The distribution of TTT through MGFs/transforms is in Topic 6.)

    Watch out

    The random-sum formulas need NNN independent of the summands. When NNN is the stopping time of the same rolls ("roll until a 6"), condition on N=nN=nN=n yourself: the first n−1n-1n−1 rolls are then conditioned to be non-stopping values, so their conditional mean changes (MS25.A1, H26-07.2). Also: Var(T)≠E[N]Var(X)\mathrm{Var}(T)\ne E[N]\mathrm{Var}(X)Var(T)=E[N]Var(X) alone; the second term is the variability of NNN.

    ES25.4Mixture X = YZ: E[X] and fX 2025 End-sem · Q4 · 10 marks★ Must-do
    Let ZZZ be a discrete random variable taking values in {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\}{1,…,n} with P(Z=i)=pi,i=1,…,n.\mathbb P(Z=i)=p_i,\quad i=1,\dots,n.P(Z=i)=pi​,i=1,…,n. Conditioned on Z=iZ=iZ=i, let XXX be distributed as YiY_iYi​. Thus we define X=YZX=Y_ZX=YZ​. Find E[X]E[X]E[X] (5 mks). Also prove that fX(x)=∑i=1npifYi(x)f_X(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i f_{Y_i}(x)fX​(x)=∑i=1n​pi​fYi​​(x). (5 mks)

    (a) E[X]E[X]E[X]

    By the law of total (iterated) expectation, E[X]=E[E[X∣Z]]E[X]=E\big[E[X\mid Z]\big]E[X]=E[E[X∣Z]]. Given Z=iZ=iZ=i, XXX has the same distribution as YiY_iYi​, so E[X∣Z=i]=E[Yi]E[X\mid Z=i]=E[Y_i]E[X∣Z=i]=E[Yi​]. Averaging over ZZZ: E[X]=∑i=1nP(Z=i) E[X∣Z=i]=∑i=1npi E[Yi].E[X]=\sum_{i=1}^nP(Z=i)\,E[X\mid Z=i]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,E[Y_i].E[X]=i=1∑n​P(Z=i)E[X∣Z=i]=i=1∑n​pi​E[Yi​].

    (b) fXf_XfX​

    The events {Z=i}\{Z=i\}{Z=i}, i=1,…,ni=1,\dots,ni=1,…,n, partition Ω\OmegaΩ. By the law of total probability, for every xxx, FX(x)=P(X≤x)=∑i=1nP(Z=i) P(X≤x∣Z=i)=∑i=1npi FYi(x),F_X(x)=P(X\le x)=\sum_{i=1}^n P(Z=i)\,P(X\le x\mid Z=i)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,F_{Y_i}(x),FX​(x)=P(X≤x)=i=1∑n​P(Z=i)P(X≤x∣Z=i)=i=1∑n​pi​FYi​​(x), since X∣{Z=i}X\mid\{Z=i\}X∣{Z=i} has the law of YiY_iYi​. Differentiating (a finite sum) gives fX(x)=∑i=1nP(Z=i) fX∣Z=i(x)=∑i=1npi fYi(x).f_X(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n P(Z=i)\,f_{X\mid Z=i}(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\,f_{Y_i}(x).fX​(x)=i=1∑n​P(Z=i)fX∣Z=i​(x)=i=1∑n​pi​fYi​​(x).

    Answer

    E[X]=∑i=1npiE[Yi]E[X]=\sum_{i=1}^n p_iE[Y_i]E[X]=∑i=1n​pi​E[Yi​] and fX(x)=∑i=1npifYi(x)f_X(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n p_if_{Y_i}(x)fX​(x)=∑i=1n​pi​fYi​​(x).

    ES22.1Geometric number of exponential terms: E[T] 2022 End-sem · Q1 · marks not shown★ Must-do
    [Reconstructed] Let T=∑i=1NXiT=\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_iT=∑i=1N​Xi​, where X1,X2,…X_1,X_2,\dotsX1​,X2​,… are i.i.d. Exponential(λ)\text{Exponential}(\lambda)Exponential(λ) random variables and N∼Geometric(p)N\sim\text{Geometric}(p)N∼Geometric(p) is independent of the XiX_iXi​. Find E[T]E[T]E[T].

    Only the key of this paper exists; the wording is reconstructed from it, the data and what is asked are as in the key.

    Solution · follows the official key

    Use the law of iterated expectation: E[T]=E[E[T∣N]]E[T]=E\big[E[T\mid N]\big]E[T]=E[E[T∣N]].

    Given N=nN=nN=n (and NNN independent of the XiX_iXi​), TTT is the fixed sum X1+⋯+XnX_1+\dots+X_nX1​+⋯+Xn​: E[T∣N=n]=E[∑i=1nXi]=nE[X](the Xi are i.i.d.),E[T\mid N=n]=E\Big[\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\Big]=nE[X]\qquad(\text{the } X_i \text{ are i.i.d.}),E[T∣N=n]=E[i=1∑n​Xi​]=nE[X](the Xi​ are i.i.d.), so E[T∣N]=N E[X]E[T\mid N]=N\,E[X]E[T∣N]=NE[X]. Taking expectations, with E[X]E[X]E[X] a constant: E[T]=E[N E[X]]=E[N] E[X].E[T]=E\big[N\,E[X]\big]=E[N]\,E[X].E[T]=E[NE[X]]=E[N]E[X]. For N∼N\simN∼ Geometric(p)(p)(p) on {1,2,… }\{1,2,\dots\}{1,2,…}, E[N]=1pE[N]=\frac1pE[N]=p1​; for X∼X\simX∼ Exp(λ)(\lambda)(λ), E[X]=1λE[X]=\frac1\lambdaE[X]=λ1​.

    Answer

    E[T]=E[N]E[X]=1pλE[T]=E[N]E[X]=\dfrac{1}{p\lambda}E[T]=E[N]E[X]=pλ1​. (In fact T∼T\simT∼ Exp(pλ)(p\lambda)(pλ), but that needs MGFs: Topic 6.)

    What the grader checks
    • E[T]=E[E[T∣N]]E[T]=E[E[T\mid N]]E[T]=E[E[T∣N]] stated.
    • E[T∣N=n]=nE[X]E[T\mid N=n]=nE[X]E[T∣N=n]=nE[X] with the reason "XiX_iXi​ i.i.d. (and independent of NNN)", hence E[T∣N]=NE[X]E[T\mid N]=NE[X]E[T∣N]=NE[X].
    • Pulling the constant E[X]E[X]E[X] out: E[N]E[X]E[N]E[X]E[N]E[X].
    • E[N]=1/pE[N]=1/pE[N]=1/p, E[X]=1/λE[X]=1/\lambdaE[X]=1/λ, final 1/(pλ)1/(p\lambda)1/(pλ).

    MS25.A1Roll until a six: expected total reward 2025 Midsem · 6-mark Q1 · 6 marks★ Must-do
    Consider the following game with a fair die. You repeatedly roll a fair die until you get a six. The game ends, when 6 appears. The reward from each roll is the face value except that a roll of 6 yields reward 0. Find the expected total reward from the game.

    Same as: midsem sample bank SB.A1. Compare H26-07.2 (same idea, stop at a 1 and count it).

    Solution · follows the official key

    Let NNN be the roll on which the first 6 appears, N∼N\simN∼ Geometric(16)(\frac16)(61​), pN(n)=(56)n−116p_N(n)=(\frac56)^{n-1}\frac16pN​(n)=(65​)n−161​, E[N]=6E[N]=6E[N]=6. The total reward is Y=R1+⋯+RNY=R_1+\dots+R_NY=R1​+⋯+RN​, where RkR_kRk​ is the reward of roll kkk and RN=0R_N=0RN​=0.

    Conditional mean given N=nN=nN=n

    The event {N=n}\{N=n\}{N=n} says: rolls 1,…,n−11,\dots,n-11,…,n−1 are not 6 and roll nnn is a 6. By independence of the rolls, each of the first n−1n-1n−1 rolls is, given this, uniform on {1,…,5}\{1,\dots,5\}{1,…,5}, with mean 1+2+3+4+55=3\frac{1+2+3+4+5}{5}=351+2+3+4+5​=3; the last roll gives 0. By linearity, E[Y∣N=n]=3(n−1),soE[Y∣N]=3(N−1).E[Y\mid N=n]=3(n-1),\qquad\text{so}\qquad E[Y\mid N]=3(N-1).E[Y∣N=n]=3(n−1),soE[Y∣N]=3(N−1).

    Method 1: law of iterated expectation

    E[Y]=E[E[Y∣N]]=3(E[N]−1)=3(6−1)=15.E[Y]=E\big[E[Y\mid N]\big]=3\big(E[N]-1\big)=3(6-1)=15.E[Y]=E[E[Y∣N]]=3(E[N]−1)=3(6−1)=15.

    Method 2: total expectation as a series

    E[Y]=∑n=1∞3(n−1)(56)n−116=12∑m=0∞m(56)m=12⋅5/6(1/6)2=12⋅30=15,E[Y]=\sum_{n=1}^\infty 3(n-1)\Big(\frac56\Big)^{n-1}\frac16=\frac12\sum_{m=0}^\infty m\Big(\frac56\Big)^m=\frac12\cdot\frac{5/6}{(1/6)^2}=\frac12\cdot30=15,E[Y]=n=1∑∞​3(n−1)(65​)n−161​=21​m=0∑∞​m(65​)m=21​⋅(1/6)25/6​=21​⋅30=15, using ∑m≥0mrm=r(1−r)2\sum_{m\ge0} mr^m=\frac{r}{(1-r)^2}∑m≥0​mrm=(1−r)2r​ for ∣r∣<1|r|\lt1∣r∣<1. (Monte Carlo: 15.02.)

    Answer

    Expected total reward =15=15=15.

    Watch out

    E[N]⋅E[R]=6⋅156=15E[N]\cdot E[R]=6\cdot\frac{15}{6}=15E[N]⋅E[R]=6⋅615​=15 happens to give the same number here (Wald's identity), but the shortcut "E[Rk∣N=n]=3.5E[R_k\mid N=n]=3.5E[Rk​∣N=n]=3.5" is wrong: conditioning on N=nN=nN=n changes the law of the earlier rolls to uniform on {1..5}\{1..5\}{1..5}.

    What the grader checks (6 marks, no split printed)
    • Total reward as a random sum over N∼N\simN∼ Geom(1/6)(1/6)(1/6).
    • Conditioning on N=nN=nN=n: first n−1n-1n−1 rolls uniform on {1..5}\{1..5\}{1..5} (mean 3), last roll 0, so E[Y∣N]=3(N−1)E[Y\mid N]=3(N-1)E[Y∣N]=3(N−1).
    • Either the series with ∑mrm\sum mr^m∑mrm or LIE with E[N]=6E[N]=6E[N]=6; answer 15.

    Key: 2025 Midsem key, pp. 1–2.

    MS26.4Gaussian mixture: PDF, E[X | I], E[X], E[X²] 2026 Midsem · Q4(a)–(c) · marks not printed★ Must-do
    (a) Gaussian Mixtures: Let I∼Bernoulli(p)I\sim\text{Bernoulli}(p)I∼Bernoulli(p), and let X1∼N(μ1,σ12),X0∼N(μ0,σ02),X_1\sim N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2),\qquad X_0\sim N(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2),X1​∼N(μ1​,σ12​),X0​∼N(μ0​,σ02​), where X0X_0X0​, X1X_1X1​, and III are mutually independent. Define X=IX1+(1−I)X0X=IX_1+(1-I)X_0X=IX1​+(1−I)X0​. Find the PDF fX(x)f_X(x)fX​(x) of XXX.
    (b) Find E[X∣I]E[X\mid I]E[X∣I] and use the law of iterated expectation to find E[X]E[X]E[X].
    (c) Find E[X2∣I]E[X^2\mid I]E[X2∣I] and use the law of iterated expectation to find E[X2]E[X^2]E[X2].

    Same as: midsem sample bank SB.A11.

    Solution · follows the official key

    (a)

    Condition on III (law of total probability): fX(x)=fX∣I(x∣1)P(I=1)+fX∣I(x∣0)P(I=0).f_X(x)=f_{X\mid I}(x\mid1)P(I=1)+f_{X\mid I}(x\mid0)P(I=0).fX​(x)=fX∣I​(x∣1)P(I=1)+fX∣I​(x∣0)P(I=0). Given I=1I=1I=1, X=X1X=X_1X=X1​; since III is independent of X1X_1X1​, conditioning on I=1I=1I=1 does not change the law of X1X_1X1​, so fX∣I(x∣1)=fX1(x)f_{X\mid I}(x\mid1)=f_{X_1}(x)fX∣I​(x∣1)=fX1​​(x). Likewise fX∣I(x∣0)=fX0(x)f_{X\mid I}(x\mid0)=f_{X_0}(x)fX∣I​(x∣0)=fX0​​(x). Hence, for all real xxx, fX(x)=p 12πσ12e−(x−μ1)22σ12+(1−p) 12πσ02e−(x−μ0)22σ02.f_X(x)=p\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_1^2}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}}+(1-p)\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma_0^2}}e^{-\frac{(x-\mu_0)^2}{2\sigma_0^2}}.fX​(x)=p2πσ12​​1​e−2σ12​(x−μ1​)2​+(1−p)2πσ02​​1​e−2σ02​(x−μ0​)2​.

    (b)

    E[X∣I=1]=E[X1]=μ1E[X\mid I=1]=E[X_1]=\mu_1E[X∣I=1]=E[X1​]=μ1​, E[X∣I=0]=E[X0]=μ0E[X\mid I=0]=E[X_0]=\mu_0E[X∣I=0]=E[X0​]=μ0​. As a random variable, E[X∣I]=Iμ1+(1−I)μ0.E[X\mid I]=I\mu_1+(1-I)\mu_0.E[X∣I]=Iμ1​+(1−I)μ0​. Law of iterated expectation, with E[I]=pE[I]=pE[I]=p: E[X]=E[Iμ1+(1−I)μ0]=pμ1+(1−p)μ0.E[X]=E\big[I\mu_1+(1-I)\mu_0\big]=p\mu_1+(1-p)\mu_0.E[X]=E[Iμ1​+(1−I)μ0​]=pμ1​+(1−p)μ0​.

    (c)

    E[X2∣I=1]=E[X12]=Var(X1)+(E[X1])2=σ12+μ12E[X^2\mid I=1]=E[X_1^2]=\mathrm{Var}(X_1)+(E[X_1])^2=\sigma_1^2+\mu_1^2E[X2∣I=1]=E[X12​]=Var(X1​)+(E[X1​])2=σ12​+μ12​, and similarly σ02+μ02\sigma_0^2+\mu_0^2σ02​+μ02​ for I=0I=0I=0. So E[X2∣I]=I(σ12+μ12)+(1−I)(σ02+μ02),E[X2]=p(σ12+μ12)+(1−p)(σ02+μ02).E[X^2\mid I]=I(\sigma_1^2+\mu_1^2)+(1-I)(\sigma_0^2+\mu_0^2),\qquad E[X^2]=p(\sigma_1^2+\mu_1^2)+(1-p)(\sigma_0^2+\mu_0^2).E[X2∣I]=I(σ12​+μ12​)+(1−I)(σ02​+μ02​),E[X2]=p(σ12​+μ12​)+(1−p)(σ02​+μ02​). (Then Var(X)=E[X2]−(E[X])2=pσ12+(1−p)σ02+p(1−p)(μ1−μ0)2\mathrm{Var}(X)=E[X^2]-(E[X])^2=p\sigma_1^2+(1-p)\sigma_0^2+p(1-p)(\mu_1-\mu_0)^2Var(X)=E[X2]−(E[X])2=pσ12​+(1−p)σ02​+p(1−p)(μ1​−μ0​)2, which is the law of total variance.)

    Answer

    fX=p ϕμ1,σ12+(1−p) ϕμ0,σ02f_X=p\,\phi_{\mu_1,\sigma_1^2}+(1-p)\,\phi_{\mu_0,\sigma_0^2}fX​=pϕμ1​,σ12​​+(1−p)ϕμ0​,σ02​​; E[X∣I]=Iμ1+(1−I)μ0E[X\mid I]=I\mu_1+(1-I)\mu_0E[X∣I]=Iμ1​+(1−I)μ0​, E[X]=pμ1+(1−p)μ0E[X]=p\mu_1+(1-p)\mu_0E[X]=pμ1​+(1−p)μ0​; E[X2]=p(σ12+μ12)+(1−p)(σ02+μ02)E[X^2]=p(\sigma_1^2+\mu_1^2)+(1-p)(\sigma_0^2+\mu_0^2)E[X2]=p(σ12​+μ12​)+(1−p)(σ02​+μ02​).

    Watch out

    XXX is not Gaussian (it can be bimodal), and it is not pX1+(1−p)X0pX_1+(1-p)X_0pX1​+(1−p)X0​. Do not add the two densities without the weights p,1−pp,1-pp,1−p.

    What the grader checks (no marks printed for Q4)
    • (a) Total probability over III, and the independence of III from X0,X1X_0,X_1X0​,X1​ used to identify fX∣I(⋅∣i)=fXif_{X\mid I}(\cdot\mid i)=f_{X_i}fX∣I​(⋅∣i)=fXi​​; explicit Gaussian formula.
    • (b) E[X∣I=1]E[X\mid I=1]E[X∣I=1], E[X∣I=0]E[X\mid I=0]E[X∣I=0], then the random variable E[X∣I]=Iμ1+(1−I)μ0E[X\mid I]=I\mu_1+(1-I)\mu_0E[X∣I]=Iμ1​+(1−I)μ0​, then E[I]=pE[I]=pE[I]=p.
    • (c) Same, with E[Xi2]=σi2+μi2E[X_i^2]=\sigma_i^2+\mu_i^2E[Xi2​]=σi2​+μi2​.

    T26-07.3Prove the law of total variance 2026 Tut 7 Q3
    If XXX and YYY are arbitrary random variables for which the necessary expectations and variances exist, then prove that Var(Y)=E[Var(Y∣X)]+Var[E(Y∣X)]\mathrm{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)]+\mathrm{Var}[\mathbb{E}(Y\mid X)]Var(Y)=E[Var(Y∣X)]+Var[E(Y∣X)].
    Solution · written for this guide

    Let g(X)=E[Y∣X]g(X)=E[Y\mid X]g(X)=E[Y∣X]. By definition of the conditional variance (the variance of the conditional distribution), Var(Y∣X)=E[Y2∣X]−g(X)2.\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)=E[Y^2\mid X]-g(X)^2.Var(Y∣X)=E[Y2∣X]−g(X)2. First term. Take expectations and use the law of iterated expectation on Y2Y^2Y2: E[Var(Y∣X)]=E[E[Y2∣X]]−E[g(X)2]=E[Y2]−E[g(X)2].E\big[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)\big]=E\big[E[Y^2\mid X]\big]-E\big[g(X)^2\big]=E[Y^2]-E\big[g(X)^2\big].E[Var(Y∣X)]=E[E[Y2∣X]]−E[g(X)2]=E[Y2]−E[g(X)2]. Second term. g(X)g(X)g(X) is a random variable with E[g(X)]=E[E[Y∣X]]=E[Y]E[g(X)]=E[E[Y\mid X]]=E[Y]E[g(X)]=E[E[Y∣X]]=E[Y] (law of iterated expectation), so Var(E[Y∣X])=E[g(X)2]−(E[g(X)])2=E[g(X)2]−(E[Y])2.\mathrm{Var}\big(E[Y\mid X]\big)=E\big[g(X)^2\big]-\big(E[g(X)]\big)^2=E\big[g(X)^2\big]-(E[Y])^2.Var(E[Y∣X])=E[g(X)2]−(E[g(X)])2=E[g(X)2]−(E[Y])2. Add. The E[g(X)2]E[g(X)^2]E[g(X)2] terms cancel: E[Var(Y∣X)]+Var(E[Y∣X])=E[Y2]−(E[Y])2=Var(Y).■E\big[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)\big]+\mathrm{Var}\big(E[Y\mid X]\big)=E[Y^2]-(E[Y])^2=\mathrm{Var}(Y).\qquad\blacksquareE[Var(Y∣X)]+Var(E[Y∣X])=E[Y2]−(E[Y])2=Var(Y).■

    Answer

    Var(Y)=E[Var(Y∣X)]+Var(E[Y∣X])\mathrm{Var}(Y)=E[\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid X)]+\mathrm{Var}(E[Y\mid X])Var(Y)=E[Var(Y∣X)]+Var(E[Y∣X]), using only Var(W)=E[W2]−(EW)2\mathrm{Var}(W)=E[W^2]-(EW)^2Var(W)=E[W2]−(EW)2 (conditionally and unconditionally) and E[E[⋅∣X]]=E[⋅]E[E[\cdot\mid X]]=E[\cdot]E[E[⋅∣X]]=E[⋅].

    H26-07.2Roll until a 1 appears: expected sum of all faces 2026 HW 7 Q2
    A fair die is rolled repeatedly until a 1 appears. Let NNN be the number of rolls needed (including the roll that shows 1), and let SSS be the sum of all face values obtained during the game, including the final roll of 1. Find E[S]\mathbb{E}[S]E[S] using the law of iterated expectation.
    Solution · written for this guide

    N∼N\simN∼ Geometric(16)(\frac16)(61​) on {1,2,… }\{1,2,\dots\}{1,2,…}, E[N]=6E[N]=6E[N]=6. Write S=R1+⋯+RNS=R_1+\dots+R_NS=R1​+⋯+RN​.

    Given N=nN=nN=n. {N=n}={R1≠1,…,Rn−1≠1, Rn=1}\{N=n\}=\{R_1\ne1,\dots,R_{n-1}\ne1,\ R_n=1\}{N=n}={R1​=1,…,Rn−1​=1, Rn​=1}. The rolls are independent, so given this event each RkR_kRk​ (k<nk\lt nk<n) is uniform on {2,…,6}\{2,\dots,6\}{2,…,6}, with mean 2+3+4+5+65=4\frac{2+3+4+5+6}{5}=452+3+4+5+6​=4, and Rn=1R_n=1Rn​=1. By linearity, E[S∣N=n]=4(n−1)+1,soE[S∣N]=4N−3.E[S\mid N=n]=4(n-1)+1,\qquad\text{so}\qquad E[S\mid N]=4N-3.E[S∣N=n]=4(n−1)+1,soE[S∣N]=4N−3. Law of iterated expectation. E[S]=E[E[S∣N]]=4E[N]−3=24−3=21.E[S]=E\big[E[S\mid N]\big]=4E[N]-3=24-3=21.E[S]=E[E[S∣N]]=4E[N]−3=24−3=21. Check with Wald: E[S]=E[N] E[R]=6⋅3.5=21E[S]=E[N]\,E[R]=6\cdot3.5=21E[S]=E[N]E[R]=6⋅3.5=21. (Monte Carlo: 20.96.)

    Answer

    E[S]=21E[S]=21E[S]=21.

    PC5.4.14V = Var(X | Y) and a check of the law of total variance PC §5.4 Problem 14
    Let XXX, YYY, and Z=E[X∣Y]Z=E[X\mid Y]Z=E[X∣Y] be as in Problem 13 (PC5.4.13). Define the random variable VVV as V=Var(X∣Y)V=\mathrm{Var}(X\mid Y)V=Var(X∣Y).
    1. Find the PMF of VVV.
    2. Find EVEVEV.
    3. Check that Var(X)=EV+Var(Z)\mathrm{Var}(X)=EV+\mathrm{Var}(Z)Var(X)=EV+Var(Z).
    Solution · written for this guide

    From PC5.4.13: given Y=yY=yY=y, XXX is Bernoulli with success probability zy=E[X∣Y=y]∈{37,12,23}z_y=E[X\mid Y=y]\in\{\frac37,\frac12,\frac23\}zy​=E[X∣Y=y]∈{73​,21​,32​} for y=0,1,2y=0,1,2y=0,1,2, and pY=(724,13,38)p_Y=(\frac7{24},\frac13,\frac38)pY​=(247​,31​,83​).

    (a)

    A Bernoulli(z)(z)(z) variance is z(1−z)z(1-z)z(1−z), so V=Z(1−Z)V=Z(1-Z)V=Z(1−Z): 37⋅47=1249\frac37\cdot\frac47=\frac{12}{49}73​⋅74​=4912​, 14\frac1441​, 23⋅13=29\frac23\cdot\frac13=\frac2932​⋅31​=92​. These are distinct, so PV(1249)=724,PV(14)=13,PV(29)=38.P_V\big(\tfrac{12}{49}\big)=\tfrac{7}{24},\qquad P_V\big(\tfrac14\big)=\tfrac13,\qquad P_V\big(\tfrac29\big)=\tfrac38.PV​(4912​)=247​,PV​(41​)=31​,PV​(92​)=83​.

    (b)

    EV=1249⋅724+14⋅13+29⋅38=114+112+112=521.EV=\frac{12}{49}\cdot\frac7{24}+\frac14\cdot\frac13+\frac29\cdot\frac38=\frac1{14}+\frac1{12}+\frac1{12}=\frac{5}{21}.EV=4912​⋅247​+41​⋅31​+92​⋅83​=141​+121​+121​=215​.

    (c)

    X∼X\simX∼ Bernoulli(1324)(\frac{13}{24})(2413​), so Var(X)=1324⋅1124=143576\mathrm{Var}(X)=\frac{13}{24}\cdot\frac{11}{24}=\frac{143}{576}Var(X)=2413​⋅2411​=576143​. With Var(Z)=414032\mathrm{Var}(Z)=\frac{41}{4032}Var(Z)=403241​ from PC5.4.13: EV+Var(Z)=9604032+414032=10014032=143576=Var(X). ✓EV+\mathrm{Var}(Z)=\frac{960}{4032}+\frac{41}{4032}=\frac{1001}{4032}=\frac{143}{576}=\mathrm{Var}(X).\ \checkmarkEV+Var(Z)=4032960​+403241​=40321001​=576143​=Var(X). ✓

    Answer

    V∈{1249,14,29}V\in\{\frac{12}{49},\frac14,\frac29\}V∈{4912​,41​,92​} w.p. 724,13,38\frac7{24},\frac13,\frac38247​,31​,83​; EV=521EV=\frac5{21}EV=215​; 521+414032=143576=Var(X)\frac5{21}+\frac{41}{4032}=\frac{143}{576}=\mathrm{Var}(X)215​+403241​=576143​=Var(X).

Mean. EY=E[E[Y∣N]]=E[N]λ=βλEY=E[E[Y\mid N]]=\frac{E[N]}\lambda=\frac\beta\lambdaEY=E[E[Y∣N]]=λE[N]​=λβ​.
    Variance. Law of total variance: Var(Y)=E[Nλ2]+Var(Nλ)=βλ2+βλ2=2βλ2.\mathrm{Var}(Y)=E\Big[\frac N{\lambda^2}\Big]+\mathrm{Var}\Big(\frac N\lambda\Big)=\frac{\beta}{\lambda^2}+\frac{\beta}{\lambda^2}=\frac{2\beta}{\lambda^2}.Var(Y)=E[λ2N​]+Var(λN​)=λ2β​+λ2β​=λ22β​. (N=0N=0N=0 gives Y=0Y=0Y=0, consistent with both formulas.)

    PC5.4.25Y | X ~ Uniform(0, X) with X ~ Exp(1): mean and variance PC §5.4 Problem 25
    Suppose X∼X\simX∼ Exponential(1)(1)(1) and given X=xX=xX=x, YYY is a uniform random variable in [0,x][0,x][0,x], i.e., Y∣X=x∼Y\mid X=x\simY∣X=x∼ Uniform(0,x)(0,x)(0,x), or equivalently Y∣X∼Y\mid X\simY∣X∼ Uniform(0,X)(0,X)(0,X).

For X∼X\simX∼ Exp(1): E[X]=1E[X]=1E[X]=1, Var(X)=1\mathrm{Var}(X)=1Var(X)=1, E[X2]=2E[X^2]=2E[X2]=2.

Check via second moments: E[Y2]=E[E[Y2∣X]]=E[X2/3]=23E[Y^2]=E[E[Y^2\mid X]]=E[X^2/3]=\frac23E[Y2]=E[E[Y2∣X]]=E[X2/3]=32​, and 23−14=512\frac23-\frac14=\frac5{12}32​−41​=125​.

    BT4.27Coin with a random bias Q: mean, covariance, variance of the head count B&T Ch. 4 Problem 27
    We toss nnn times a biased coin whose probability of heads, denoted by qqq, is the value of a random variable QQQ with given mean μ\muμ and positive variance σ2\sigma^2σ2. Let XiX_iXi​ be a Bernoulli random variable that models the outcome of the iiith toss (i.e., Xi=1X_i=1Xi​=1 if the iiith toss is a head). We assume that X1,…,XnX_1,\dots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ are conditionally independent, given Q=qQ=qQ=q. Let XXX be the number of heads obtained in the nnn tosses.
    1. Use the law of iterated expectations to find E[Xi]E[X_i]E[Xi​] and E[X]E[X]E[X].
    2. Find cov(Xi,Xj)\mathrm{cov}(X_i,X_j)cov(Xi​,Xj​). Are X1,…,XnX_1,\dots,X_nX1​,…,Xn​ independent?
    3. Use the law of total variance to find var(X)\mathrm{var}(X)var(X). Verify your answer using the covariance result of part (b).
    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    (a)

    E[Xi∣Q]=QE[X_i\mid Q]=QE[Xi​∣Q]=Q, so E[Xi]=E[E[Xi∣Q]]=E[Q]=μE[X_i]=E[E[X_i\mid Q]]=E[Q]=\muE[Xi​]=E[E[Xi​∣Q]]=E[Q]=μ, and E[X]=∑iE[Xi]=nμE[X]=\sum_iE[X_i]=n\muE[X]=∑i​E[Xi​]=nμ.

    (b)

    For i≠ji\ne ji=j, by conditional independence E[XiXj∣Q]=E[Xi∣Q]E[Xj∣Q]=Q2E[X_iX_j\mid Q]=E[X_i\mid Q]E[X_j\mid Q]=Q^2E[Xi​Xj​∣Q]=E[Xi​∣Q]E[Xj​∣Q]=Q2, so E[XiXj]=E[Q2]=σ2+μ2,cov(Xi,Xj)=σ2+μ2−μ2=σ2>0.E[X_iX_j]=E[Q^2]=\sigma^2+\mu^2,\qquad \mathrm{cov}(X_i,X_j)=\sigma^2+\mu^2-\mu^2=\sigma^2\gt0.E[Xi​Xj​]=E[Q2]=σ2+μ2,cov(Xi​,Xj​)=σ2+μ2−μ2=σ2>0. Nonzero covariance, so the XiX_iXi​ are not independent (a head makes a large QQQ more likely). Also Xi2=XiX_i^2=X_iXi2​=Xi​ gives var(Xi)=μ−μ2\mathrm{var}(X_i)=\mu-\mu^2var(Xi​)=μ−μ2.

    (c)

    Given QQQ, X∼X\simX∼ Binomial(n,Q)(n,Q)(n,Q): E[X∣Q]=nQE[X\mid Q]=nQE[X∣Q]=nQ, var(X∣Q)=nQ(1−Q)\mathrm{var}(X\mid Q)=nQ(1-Q)var(X∣Q)=nQ(1−Q). Law of total variance: var(X)=E[nQ(1−Q)]+var(nQ)=n(μ−σ2−μ2)+n2σ2=n(μ−μ2)+n(n−1)σ2,\mathrm{var}(X)=E[nQ(1-Q)]+\mathrm{var}(nQ)=n\big(\mu-\sigma^2-\mu^2\big)+n^2\sigma^2=n(\mu-\mu^2)+n(n-1)\sigma^2,var(X)=E[nQ(1−Q)]+var(nQ)=n(μ−σ2−μ2)+n2σ2=n(μ−μ2)+n(n−1)σ2, using E[Q2]=σ2+μ2E[Q^2]=\sigma^2+\mu^2E[Q2]=σ2+μ2. Check with (b): var(X)=∑ivar(Xi)+∑i≠jcov(Xi,Xj)=n(μ−μ2)+n(n−1)σ2\mathrm{var}(X)=\sum_i\mathrm{var}(X_i)+\sum_{i\ne j}\mathrm{cov}(X_i,X_j)=n(\mu-\mu^2)+n(n-1)\sigma^2var(X)=∑i​var(Xi​)+∑i=j​cov(Xi​,Xj​)=n(μ−μ2)+n(n−1)σ2. ✓\checkmark✓ (Monte Carlo with Q∼Q\simQ∼ U(0,1), n=5n=5n=5: formula 35/12≈2.91735/12\approx2.91735/12≈2.917, simulation 2.9122.9122.912.)

    Answer

    E[X]=nμE[X]=n\muE[X]=nμ; cov(Xi,Xj)=σ2\mathrm{cov}(X_i,X_j)=\sigma^2cov(Xi​,Xj​)=σ2 (not independent); var(X)=n(μ−μ2)+n(n−1)σ2\mathrm{var}(X)=n(\mu-\mu^2)+n(n-1)\sigma^2var(X)=n(μ−μ2)+n(n−1)σ2.

    5  Bayes' rule and total probability with random variables · Lecture 13

    Theory recap

    The inference picture from the lecture: an unobserved XXX with known law fXf_XfX​ (the prior), a measurement YYY with known fY∣Xf_{Y\mid X}fY∣X​. Total probability gives the law of the measurement; Bayes' rule turns it around to fX∣Yf_{X\mid Y}fX∣Y​ (the posterior). Either variable may be discrete or continuous; the formulas are the same with sums for PMFs and integrals for PDFs.

    Total probability over a random parameter

    If Λ\LambdaΛ has density fΛf_\LambdafΛ​ and, given Λ=λ\Lambda=\lambdaΛ=λ, XXX has PMF pX∣Λ(x∣λ)p_{X\mid\Lambda}(x\mid\lambda)pX∣Λ​(x∣λ): pX(x)=∫pX∣Λ(x∣λ)fΛ(λ) dλ,P(A)=∫P(A∣Λ=λ)fΛ(λ) dλ.p_X(x)=\int p_{X\mid\Lambda}(x\mid\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)\,d\lambda,\qquad P(A)=\int P(A\mid\Lambda=\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)\,d\lambda.pX​(x)=∫pX∣Λ​(x∣λ)fΛ​(λ)dλ,P(A)=∫P(A∣Λ=λ)fΛ​(λ)dλ. With a discrete parameter NNN: pX(x)=∑npX∣N(x∣n)pN(n)p_X(x)=\sum_n p_{X\mid N}(x\mid n)p_N(n)pX​(x)=∑n​pX∣N​(x∣n)pN​(n). The support of the sum/integral matters (e.g. n≥xn\ge xn≥x for a binomial given N=nN=nN=n).

    Bayes' rule, four versions

    fX∣Y(x∣y)=fY∣X(y∣x)fX(x)∫fY∣X(y∣t)fX(t) dt,pX∣Y(x∣y)=pY∣X(y∣x)pX(x)∑ipY∣X(y∣i)pX(i),f_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)f_X(x)}{\int f_{Y\mid X}(y\mid t)f_X(t)\,dt},\qquad p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=\frac{p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x)}{\sum_i p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid i)p_X(i)},fX∣Y​(x∣y)=∫fY∣X​(y∣t)fX​(t)dtfY∣X​(y∣x)fX​(x)​,pX∣Y​(x∣y)=∑i​pY∣X​(y∣i)pX​(i)pY∣X​(y∣x)pX​(x)​, P(N=n∣Y=y)=fY∣N(y∣n)pN(n)∑ifY∣N(y∣i)pN(i),fY∣N(y∣n)=P(N=n∣Y=y)fY(y)∫P(N=n∣Y=t)fY(t) dt.P(N=n\mid Y=y)=\frac{f_{Y\mid N}(y\mid n)p_N(n)}{\sum_i f_{Y\mid N}(y\mid i)p_N(i)},\qquad f_{Y\mid N}(y\mid n)=\frac{P(N=n\mid Y=y)f_Y(y)}{\int P(N=n\mid Y=t)f_Y(t)\,dt}.P(N=n∣Y=y)=∑i​fY∣N​(y∣i)pN​(i)fY∣N​(y∣n)pN​(n)​,fY∣N​(y∣n)=∫P(N=n∣Y=t)fY​(t)dtP(N=n∣Y=y)fY​(y)​. Lecture examples: bulb lifetime Y∼Y\simY∼ Exp(Λ)(\Lambda)(Λ), Λ∼U[1,1.5]\Lambda\sim U[1,1.5]Λ∼U[1,1.5]: fΛ∣Y(λ∣y)=2λe−λy∫11.52te−tydtf_{\Lambda\mid Y}(\lambda\mid y)=\frac{2\lambda e^{-\lambda y}}{\int_1^{1.5}2te^{-ty}dt}fΛ∣Y​(λ∣y)=∫11.5​2te−tydt2λe−λy​ on [1,1.5][1,1.5][1,1.5] (B&T Ex. 3.19); signal X=±1X=\pm1X=±1 plus N(0,1)N(0,1)N(0,1) noise: P(X=1∣Y=y)=peypey+(1−p)e−yP(X=1\mid Y=y)=\frac{pe^y}{pe^y+(1-p)e^{-y}}P(X=1∣Y=y)=pey+(1−p)e−ypey​ (B&T Ex. 3.20).

    The integral that finishes most of these

    ∫0∞tne−t dt=n!(n=0,1,2,… ),so∫0∞λne−aλ dλ=n!an+1 (a>0),∫01pk(1−p)n−kdp=k!(n−k)!(n+1)!.\int_0^\infty t^ne^{-t}\,dt=n!\quad(n=0,1,2,\dots),\qquad\text{so}\quad\int_0^\infty\lambda^ne^{-a\lambda}\,d\lambda=\frac{n!}{a^{n+1}}\ (a\gt0),\qquad \int_0^1p^k(1-p)^{n-k}dp=\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}.∫0∞​tne−tdt=n!(n=0,1,2,…),so∫0∞​λne−aλdλ=an+1n!​ (a>0),∫01​pk(1−p)n−kdp=(n+1)!k!(n−k)!​. Substitute t=aλt=a\lambdat=aλ; the first identity follows by repeated integration by parts.

    Watch out

    The posterior is a density in the parameter, with the parameter's support (e.g. 0≤p≤10\le p\le10≤p≤1); state it. Constant factors that do not involve the parameter cancel between numerator and denominator, so drop them early. "Given P=pP=pP=p, the tosses are independent" is an assumption you must quote when you write P(2nd head∣P=p,1st head)=pP(\text{2nd head}\mid P=p,\text{1st head})=pP(2nd head∣P=p,1st head)=p.

    RQ22.B4Poisson with an exponential rate is geometric 2022 Replacement Quiz · S2 Q4 · 5 marks★ Must-do
    Let XXX have a Poisson distribution with parameter Λ\LambdaΛ, where Λ\LambdaΛ is an exponential random variable with parameter μ\muμ. Show that XXX has a geometric distribution.
    Solution · follows the official key

    Given: fΛ(λ)=μe−μλf_\Lambda(\lambda)=\mu e^{-\mu\lambda}fΛ​(λ)=μe−μλ for λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0, and P(X=x∣Λ=λ)=e−λλxx!P(X=x\mid\Lambda=\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}\dfrac{\lambda^x}{x!}P(X=x∣Λ=λ)=e−λx!λx​ for x∈{0,1,2,… }x\in\{0,1,2,\dots\}x∈{0,1,2,…}.

    Total probability over the continuous Λ\LambdaΛ: P(X=x)=∫0∞P(X=x∣Λ=λ)fΛ(λ) dλ=∫0∞e−λλxx! μe−μλ dλ=μx!∫0∞λxe−(1+μ)λ dλ.P(X=x)=\int_0^\infty P(X=x\mid\Lambda=\lambda)f_\Lambda(\lambda)\,d\lambda=\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^x}{x!}\,\mu e^{-\mu\lambda}\,d\lambda=\frac{\mu}{x!}\int_0^\infty\lambda^xe^{-(1+\mu)\lambda}\,d\lambda.P(X=x)=∫0∞​P(X=x∣Λ=λ)fΛ​(λ)dλ=∫0∞​e−λx!λx​μe−μλdλ=x!μ​∫0∞​λxe−(1+μ)λdλ. Integrate. Put t=(1+μ)λt=(1+\mu)\lambdat=(1+μ)λ, dλ=dt1+μd\lambda=\frac{dt}{1+\mu}dλ=1+μdt​: P(X=x)=μx! (1+μ)x+1∫0∞txe−t dt.P(X=x)=\frac{\mu}{x!\,(1+\mu)^{x+1}}\int_0^\infty t^xe^{-t}\,dt.P(X=x)=x!(1+μ)x+1μ​∫0∞​txe−tdt. By parts, ∫0∞txe−tdt=[−txe−t]0∞+x∫0∞tx−1e−tdt=x∫0∞tx−1e−tdt=⋯=x(x−1)⋯1⋅∫0∞e−tdt=x!\int_0^\infty t^xe^{-t}dt=\big[-t^xe^{-t}\big]_0^\infty+x\int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}dt=x\int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}dt=\dots=x(x-1)\cdots1\cdot\int_0^\infty e^{-t}dt=x!∫0∞​txe−tdt=[−txe−t]0∞​+x∫0∞​tx−1e−tdt=x∫0∞​tx−1e−tdt=⋯=x(x−1)⋯1⋅∫0∞​e−tdt=x!. Hence P(X=x)=μ(1+μ)x+1=μ1+μ(11+μ)x,x=0,1,2,…P(X=x)=\frac{\mu}{(1+\mu)^{x+1}}=\frac{\mu}{1+\mu}\Big(\frac{1}{1+\mu}\Big)^{x},\qquad x=0,1,2,\dotsP(X=x)=(1+μ)x+1μ​=1+μμ​(1+μ1​)x,x=0,1,2,… Identify. This is q(1−q)xq(1-q)^xq(1−q)x with q=μ1+μq=\frac{\mu}{1+\mu}q=1+μμ​: the geometric distribution on {0,1,2,… }\{0,1,2,\dots\}{0,1,2,…} (number of failures before the first success) with success probability μ1+μ\frac\mu{1+\mu}1+μμ​. (Check: ∑xq(1−q)x=1\sum_x q(1-q)^x=1∑x​q(1−q)x=1.)

    Answer

    P(X=x)=μ(1+μ)x+1, x=0,1,2,…P(X=x)=\dfrac{\mu}{(1+\mu)^{x+1}},\ x=0,1,2,\dotsP(X=x)=(1+μ)x+1μ​, x=0,1,2,…: geometric with success probability μ1+μ\frac{\mu}{1+\mu}1+μμ​.

    MS24.A4Binomial(N, p) with N ~ Poisson(λ): PMF and mean 2024 Midsem · 6-mark Q4 · 6 marks★ Must-do
    Let XXX be a random variable having Binomial distribution with parameters NNN and ppp where NNN is itself a random variable having Poisson distribution with mean λ\lambdaλ. Find the probability mass function of the random variable XXX. Also find E[X]E[X]E[X].

    Same as: midsem sample bank SB.A7 and SB.B3. The same result ("splitting a Poisson") is B&T Ch. 2 Problem 37 and PC §5.1.6 Solved Problem 5; do it once here.

    Solution · follows the official key

    N∼N\simN∼ Poisson(λ)(\lambda)(λ): P(N=n)=e−λλnn!P(N=n)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}P(N=n)=e−λn!λn​, n≥0n\ge0n≥0. Given N=nN=nN=n: P(X=x∣N=n)=(nx)px(1−p)n−xP(X=x\mid N=n)=\binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x}P(X=x∣N=n)=(xn​)px(1−p)n−x for 0≤x≤n0\le x\le n0≤x≤n, and 0 for x>nx\gt nx>n.

    PMF by total probability

    For x=0,1,2,…x=0,1,2,\dotsx=0,1,2,… only n≥xn\ge xn≥x contribute: P(X=x)=∑n=x∞(nx)px(1−p)n−xe−λλnn!=e−λpxx!∑n=x∞(1−p)n−xλn(n−x)!.P(X=x)=\sum_{n=x}^\infty\binom nx p^x(1-p)^{n-x}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^n}{n!}=\frac{e^{-\lambda}p^x}{x!}\sum_{n=x}^\infty\frac{(1-p)^{n-x}\lambda^n}{(n-x)!}.P(X=x)=n=x∑∞​(xn​)px(1−p)n−xe−λn!λn​=x!e−λpx​n=x∑∞​(n−x)!(1−p)n−xλn​. Put k=n−xk=n-xk=n−x and λn=λxλk\lambda^n=\lambda^x\lambda^kλn=λxλk: P(X=x)=e−λ(λp)xx!∑k=0∞(λ(1−p))kk!=e−λ(λp)xx!eλ(1−p)=e−λp(λp)xx!.P(X=x)=\frac{e^{-\lambda}(\lambda p)^x}{x!}\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{(\lambda(1-p))^k}{k!}=\frac{e^{-\lambda}(\lambda p)^x}{x!}e^{\lambda(1-p)}=e^{-\lambda p}\frac{(\lambda p)^x}{x!}.P(X=x)=x!e−λ(λp)x​k=0∑∞​k!(λ(1−p))k​=x!e−λ(λp)x​eλ(1−p)=e−λpx!(λp)x​. So X∼X\simX∼ Poisson(λp)(\lambda p)(λp).

    Mean

    From the Poisson PMF, E[X]=λpE[X]=\lambda pE[X]=λp. Or by iterated expectation: E[X∣N]=NpE[X\mid N]=NpE[X∣N]=Np, so E[X]=E[E[X∣N]]=pE[N]=λpE[X]=E[E[X\mid N]]=pE[N]=\lambda pE[X]=E[E[X∣N]]=pE[N]=λp.

    Answer

    P(X=x)=e−λp(λp)xx!, x=0,1,…P(X=x)=e^{-\lambda p}\dfrac{(\lambda p)^x}{x!},\ x=0,1,\dotsP(X=x)=e−λpx!(λp)x​, x=0,1,… (Poisson(λp)(\lambda p)(λp)); E[X]=λpE[X]=\lambda pE[X]=λp.

    What the grader checks (6 marks)
    • Binomial and Poisson PMFs written (0.5 each).
    • Simplification: sum from n=xn=xn=x, reindex k=n−xk=n-xk=n−x, exponential series (2.5); final PMF (0.5).
    • Using the Poisson mean or the law of iterated expectation (1); final E[X]=λpE[X]=\lambda pE[X]=λp (1).

    Key: 2024 Midsem key, pp. 4–5.

    Tutorials and homeworks

    H25-06.6Geiger counter: posterior that the rate is low after 2 counts 2025 HW 6 Q6
    A Geiger counter measures background radiation. The machine's true average rate of detection, λ\lambdaλ, is known to be either low (λ1=0.1\lambda_1=0.1λ1​=0.1 counts/sec) or high (λ2=0.5\lambda_2=0.5λ2​=0.5 counts/sec). The prior probability of the rate being low is P(λ=λ1)=0.8P(\lambda=\lambda_1)=0.8P(λ=λ1​)=0.8. The number of counts KKK in a given second follows a Poisson distribution with parameter λ\lambdaλ. You turn on the counter for one second and observe exactly k=2k=2k=2 counts. What is the updated (posterior) probability that the rate is low, given your observation? That is, find P(λ=λ1∣K=2)P(\lambda=\lambda_1\mid K=2)P(λ=λ1​∣K=2).
    Solution · follows the 2025 course solutions

    Bayes' rule for a discrete parameter and a discrete observation: P(λ1∣K=2)=P(K=2∣λ1)P(λ1)P(K=2∣λ1)P(λ1)+P(K=2∣λ2)P(λ2),P(\lambda_1\mid K=2)=\frac{P(K=2\mid\lambda_1)P(\lambda_1)}{P(K=2\mid\lambda_1)P(\lambda_1)+P(K=2\mid\lambda_2)P(\lambda_2)},P(λ1​∣K=2)=P(K=2∣λ1​)P(λ1​)+P(K=2∣λ2​)P(λ2​)P(K=2∣λ1​)P(λ1​)​, the denominator being P(K=2)P(K=2)P(K=2) by total probability. Likelihoods from the Poisson PMF: P(K=2∣0.1)=e−0.1(0.1)22=0.005e−0.1,P(K=2∣0.5)=e−0.5(0.5)22=0.125e−0.5.P(K=2\mid0.1)=\frac{e^{-0.1}(0.1)^2}{2}=0.005e^{-0.1},\qquad P(K=2\mid0.5)=\frac{e^{-0.5}(0.5)^2}{2}=0.125e^{-0.5}.P(K=2∣0.1)=2e−0.1(0.1)2​=0.005e−0.1,P(K=2∣0.5)=2e−0.5(0.5)2​=0.125e−0.5. So P(λ1∣K=2)=0.004e−0.10.004e−0.1+0.025e−0.5≈0.0036190.003619+0.015163≈0.1927.P(\lambda_1\mid K=2)=\frac{0.004e^{-0.1}}{0.004e^{-0.1}+0.025e^{-0.5}}\approx\frac{0.003619}{0.003619+0.015163}\approx0.1927.P(λ1​∣K=2)=0.004e−0.1+0.025e−0.50.004e−0.1​≈0.003619+0.0151630.003619​≈0.1927. Two counts in one second are much more likely under the high rate, so the posterior moves from 0.8 down to about 0.19.

    Answer

    P(λ=0.1∣K=2)=0.004e−0.10.004e−0.1+0.025e−0.5≈0.193P(\lambda=0.1\mid K=2)=\dfrac{0.004e^{-0.1}}{0.004e^{-0.1}+0.025e^{-0.5}}\approx0.193P(λ=0.1∣K=2)=0.004e−0.1+0.025e−0.50.004e−0.1​≈0.193.

    Bertsekas & Tsitsiklis

    BT3.34Defective coin mint: random head probability, posterior, next toss B&T Ch. 3 Problem 34
    A defective coin minting machine produces coins whose probability of heads is a random variable PPP with PDF fP(p)={pep,p∈[0,1],0,otherwise.f_P(p)=\begin{cases}pe^p, & p\in[0,1],\\ 0, &\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}fP​(p)={pep,0,​p∈[0,1],otherwise.​ A coin produced by this machine is selected and tossed repeatedly, with successive tosses assumed independent.
    1. Find the probability that a coin toss results in heads.
    2. Given that a coin toss resulted in heads, find the conditional PDF of PPP.
    3. Given that the first coin toss resulted in heads, find the conditional probability of heads on the next toss.
    Solution · follows the B&T official solution

    (fPf_PfP​ is a valid density: ∫01pep dp=[ep(p−1)]01=1\int_0^1pe^p\,dp=\big[e^p(p-1)\big]_0^1=1∫01​pepdp=[ep(p−1)]01​=1.) Let AAA = first toss heads, BBB = second toss heads. Given P=pP=pP=p, the tosses are independent with head probability ppp.

    (a)

    Continuous total probability: P(A)=∫01P(A∣P=p)fP(p) dp=∫01p2ep dp=[ep(p2−2p+2)]01=e−2≈0.718.P(A)=\int_0^1P(A\mid P=p)f_P(p)\,dp=\int_0^1p^2e^p\,dp=\big[e^p(p^2-2p+2)\big]_0^1=e-2\approx0.718.P(A)=∫01​P(A∣P=p)fP​(p)dp=∫01​p2epdp=[ep(p2−2p+2)]01​=e−2≈0.718.

    (b)

    Bayes' rule: fP∣A(p)=P(A∣P=p)fP(p)P(A)=p2epe−2,0≤p≤1,0 otherwise.f_{P\mid A}(p)=\frac{P(A\mid P=p)f_P(p)}{P(A)}=\frac{p^2e^p}{e-2},\qquad 0\le p\le1,\quad 0\text{ otherwise}.fP∣A​(p)=P(A)P(A∣P=p)fP​(p)​=e−2p2ep​,0≤p≤1,0 otherwise.

    (c)

    Condition on PPP within the conditional world AAA. By conditional independence, P(B∣P=p,A)=P(B∣P=p)=pP(B\mid P=p,A)=P(B\mid P=p)=pP(B∣P=p,A)=P(B∣P=p)=p: P(B∣A)=∫01p fP∣A(p) dp=1e−2∫01p3ep dp=[ep(p3−3p2+6p−6)]01e−2=6−2ee−2≈0.784.P(B\mid A)=\int_0^1p\,f_{P\mid A}(p)\,dp=\frac{1}{e-2}\int_0^1p^3e^p\,dp=\frac{\big[e^p(p^3-3p^2+6p-6)\big]_0^1}{e-2}=\frac{6-2e}{e-2}\approx0.784.P(B∣A)=∫01​pfP∣A​(p)dp=e−21​∫01​p3epdp=e−2[ep(p3−3p2+6p−6)]01​​=e−26−2e​≈0.784.

    Answer

    P(A)=e−2P(A)=e-2P(A)=e−2; fP∣A(p)=p2epe−2f_{P\mid A}(p)=\frac{p^2e^p}{e-2}fP∣A​(p)=e−2p2ep​ on [0,1][0,1][0,1]; P(B∣A)=6−2ee−2≈0.784P(B\mid A)=\frac{6-2e}{e-2}\approx0.784P(B∣A)=e−26−2e​≈0.784.

    Official solution: B&T solutions, pp. 45–46. It prints 0.5640.718≈0.786\frac{0.564}{0.718}\approx0.7860.7180.564​≈0.786; the exact value is 0.78440.78440.7844 (the 0.786 is a rounding slip).

    BTS3.18Machine with a uniform reliability P: posterior after m of n good days B&T Supp. Ch. 3 Problem 18
    Let PPP be a random variable which is uniformly distributed between 0 and 1. On any given day, a particular machine is functional with probability PPP. Furthermore, given the value of PPP, the status of the machine on different days is independent.
    1. Find the probability that the machine is functional on a particular day.
    2. We are told that the machine was functional on mmm out of the last nnn days. Find the conditional PDF of PPP. You may use the identity ∫01pk(1−p)n−k dp=k!(n−k)!(n+1)!\displaystyle\int_0^1p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\,dp=\frac{k!(n-k)!}{(n+1)!}∫01​pk(1−p)n−kdp=(n+1)!k!(n−k)!​.
    3. Find the conditional probability that the machine is functional today given that it was functional on mmm out of the last nnn days.
    Solution · written for this guide

    fP(p)=1f_P(p)=1fP​(p)=1 on [0,1][0,1][0,1]. Let FFF = functional today, AmA_mAm​ = functional on exactly mmm of the last nnn days.

    (a)

    P(F)=∫01P(F∣P=p)fP(p) dp=∫01p dp=12P(F)=\int_0^1P(F\mid P=p)f_P(p)\,dp=\int_0^1p\,dp=\frac12P(F)=∫01​P(F∣P=p)fP​(p)dp=∫01​pdp=21​.

    (b)

    Given P=pP=pP=p, the nnn days are independent, so P(Am∣P=p)=(nm)pm(1−p)n−mP(A_m\mid P=p)=\binom nm p^m(1-p)^{n-m}P(Am​∣P=p)=(mn​)pm(1−p)n−m. Total probability and the given identity: P(Am)=(nm)∫01pm(1−p)n−mdp=(nm)m!(n−m)!(n+1)!=1n+1.P(A_m)=\binom nm\int_0^1p^m(1-p)^{n-m}dp=\binom nm\frac{m!(n-m)!}{(n+1)!}=\frac{1}{n+1}.P(Am​)=(mn​)∫01​pm(1−p)n−mdp=(mn​)(n+1)!m!(n−m)!​=n+11​. Bayes' rule: fP∣Am(p)=(nm)pm(1−p)n−m⋅11/(n+1)=(n+1)!m! (n−m)! pm(1−p)n−m,0≤p≤1,f_{P\mid A_m}(p)=\frac{\binom nm p^m(1-p)^{n-m}\cdot1}{1/(n+1)}=\frac{(n+1)!}{m!\,(n-m)!}\,p^m(1-p)^{n-m},\qquad0\le p\le1,fP∣Am​​(p)=1/(n+1)(mn​)pm(1−p)n−m⋅1​=m!(n−m)!(n+1)!​pm(1−p)n−m,0≤p≤1, and 0 otherwise (a Beta(m+1,n−m+1)(m+1,n-m+1)(m+1,n−m+1) density).

    (c)

    Given P=pP=pP=p, today is independent of the past days, so P(F∣P=p,Am)=pP(F\mid P=p,A_m)=pP(F∣P=p,Am​)=p and P(F∣Am)=∫01p fP∣Am(p) dp=(n+1)!m!(n−m)!⋅(m+1)!(n−m)!(n+2)!=m+1n+2.P(F\mid A_m)=\int_0^1p\,f_{P\mid A_m}(p)\,dp=\frac{(n+1)!}{m!(n-m)!}\cdot\frac{(m+1)!(n-m)!}{(n+2)!}=\frac{m+1}{n+2}.P(F∣Am​)=∫01​pfP∣Am​​(p)dp=m!(n−m)!(n+1)!​⋅(n+2)!(m+1)!(n−m)!​=n+2m+1​.

    Answer

    P(F)=12P(F)=\frac12P(F)=21​; fP∣Am(p)=(n+1)!m!(n−m)!pm(1−p)n−mf_{P\mid A_m}(p)=\frac{(n+1)!}{m!(n-m)!}p^m(1-p)^{n-m}fP∣Am​​(p)=m!(n−m)!(n+1)!​pm(1−p)n−m on [0,1][0,1][0,1]; P(F∣Am)=m+1n+2P(F\mid A_m)=\frac{m+1}{n+2}P(F∣Am​)=n+2m+1​ (Laplace's rule of succession).
